ANTI-INFLATION BOARD REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION OF DECISION ON WAGE SETTLEMENT OF INCO WORKERS AT THOMPSON-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from the Anti-Inflation Board roll-back of a settlement reached between United Steelworkers local 6166 and International Nickel Company of Canada which concerns a work force of
3,000	employees in Thompson, Manitoba. In view of the fact that there is a clear historic relationship between the Manitoba Division of INCO Limited and its employees and settlements between INCO Limited and its employees in Sudbury, Port Colborne and Shebandowan, Ontario, which settlements were reached prior to the implementation of AIB regulations and which historically always precede Manitoba negotiations by six months; and in view of the fact that an AIB imposed settlement in Thompson significantly lower than in the Ontario operations will result in a critical shortage of employees in Thompson, and in view of the fact that maintenance of operations in Thompson is vital to the continued existence of the city of Thompson because the INCO payroll is 80 per cent of the total payroll in that city, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to table forthwith a telegram from three thousand citizens of Northern Manitoba protesting the roll back and the Government's misleading statements in this matter, and that the Prime Minister and Cabinet immediately consider the destructive consequences of the roll back to the city of Thompson, other northern communities, and the mining industry of Canada and take appropriate steps to alleviate the situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss an urgent matter.
Since last spring the manufacturers of chemical fertilizers were not in a position to provide normal supplies to farmers; since chemical fertilizers were so expensive in 1975 that a great many farmers were unable to buy some to meet their needs; and since there were price fluctuations, even taking into consideration the location of supplies, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House take all the necessary steps in the shortest possible time to establish a special committee to undertake an immediate study on the availability and prices of chemical fertilizers and thus exercise a control on the prices of chemical fertilizers to prevent farmers from being exploited at that level and to guarantee a sufficient supply of fertilizers to meet the demand.

I agree with the conclusion the hon. member has reached that it is not likely by the end of this particular session either a partial treaty relating to fisheries or a general treaty will emerge. I made those remarks for two reasons. First, it was just at the time we had begun to operate under new procedures with respect to the question period and, second, as a new Speaker I felt hon. members would wish to know as soon as possible my attitude toward the handling of the question period. I attempted to make that statement a thorough review of my attitude toward questions that ought to be permitted. I tried to make it as positive as possible and in line with a theme different from that of the past. Instead of there being a number of restrictions such as had grown up, somewhat vaguely, affecting the right of members to put questions, I attempted to put forward a positive statement as to what could be done, rather than a negative statement expressing what could not be done.
In respect of the responsibility of ministers and the areas which could be covered, I said this as recorded at the top of page 4763 of Hansard of April 14, 1975:
Sixth, a question must be within the administrative responsibility of the government or the minister. Obviously, the government in general cannot be responsible for those areas which are beyond its own administrative responsibility. Furthermore, the minister to whom the question is directed is responsible to the House for his ministry; that is, his present ministry. He is responsible to the limits of that ministry, but not beyond that. In this regard I find no reason to change the earlier decision I made in respect of the capacities which ministers enjoyed in previously-held portfolios.
I think that statement is clear, and by and large it has not been challenged, I have to be concerned whether that ruling unduly restricts the right of members to put questions in respect of a situation facing us where information is sought about influence which members-indeed, ministers-might have exercised with respect to decisions affecting tenders. I am satisfied that the ruling I have quoted is a fair one still because, of course, questions can always be put to the Prime Minister concerning the conduct of any minister; questions can be put to the minister responsible for the tendering in the particular department involved, they can be put to the President of the Treasury Board with respect to general tendering practices, and they can certainly be put to the Solicitor General or to the Minister of Justice if there seems to be any suspicion of irregularity.
In some cases there is no doubt that questions are deflected to ministers who have served in previous capacities, but it seems to me that this is within the limits of jurisdictional responsibility as we have always known it and extends ample opportunity for hon. members to put questions at least during the question period. We have to remember, after all, that we are not attempting to afford complete investigative powers in the question period, but simply trying to manage the question period which is an extremely important aspect of our procedure and one whose duration each day is limited.
Finally, I am sure hon. members will understand that there are circumstances in which the enforcement of this rule is not easy for the Chair: ministers, in making one answer, may voluntarily go across the line and it is dif-

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENT ENTITLED "AN ENERGY STRATEGY FOR CANADA-POLICIES FOR SELF-RELIANCE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table, in both official languages, copies of a document entitled, "An Energy Strategy for Canada-Policies for Self-reliance" and a summary of the same document.
Mr. Speaker, it is now almost three years since this government published "An Energy Policy for Canada- Phase I". That publication, issued in June of 1973, presented a comprehensive overview of the Canadian energy situation, its history, prospects and problems. Our intention was to begin a process of consultation, reflection and debate which would enable us to develop a set of national energy policies.

Barely four months later, war broke out in the Middle East and the Organization of Petroleum exporting Countries raised the international price of oil substantially. In the fall of 1973, oil in the Persian Gulf sold for $2.20 a barrel. Today the price is $11.50. This fivefold increase in the price of the singlemost important energy commodity, occurring as it did in a period of less than two years, has sent a series of shockwaves through the international economic system. It has contributed directly to the worst recession in the industrialized world since the 1930s, coupled with continuing rapid inflation. No country has been unaffected.
Canada has been more fortunate than most countries. Because we have domestic oil reserves we have been able to cushion the effects of higher international prices. The price of oil in Canada is currently about $4.60 per barrel lower than the price eastern Canadians would have to pay for imported oil if there were no subsidy program. However, proved reserves of Canadian oil and low-cost proved reserves of natural gas are declining. Canada now imports more crude oil than it sells abroad. As well, drilling results in Canada's frontier areas have been disappointing and the recent experience with the Syncrude project indicates that the further development of the oil sands will be extremely expensive. Finding new oil and natural gas reserves, developing them and transporting them to market will now cost substantially more and will require Canadian prices higher than those currently existing.
While our proved reserves of oil and low-cost gas continue to decline, Canadian demands for these energy forms continue to increase. The growing gap between our energy demands and our ability to supply them from domestic reserves suggests that we could become increasingly dependent on the rest of the world, and the OPEC cartel in particular, for our future oil supplies. This prospect carries with it economic and political risks that the government views with concern.
We have, within Canada, the people, the equipment, the expertise and the potential energy resources to reduce substantially our dependence on imported oil. We can do this by reducing the rate at which our energy requirements grow in the future, by substituting those energy forms which are in relatively abundant supply in Canada for those that are not, by accelerating the search required to find new oil and natural gas-to convert the potential of our undiscovered energy resources to proved reserves from which our needs can be supplied. These options will be expensive, but all must be pursued. The alternatives are energy shortages which will require increasing dependence on high cost, insecure oil imports or rationing available supplies among Canadians. It is within our power to avoid both of these alternatives and we must act to do so.
The publication that I am tabling this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, sets forth a national energy strategy for Canada. It is a strategy that is consistent and comprehensive. The strategy consists of three well defined parts: first, an objective-energy self-reliance; second, a series of specific energy targets; and finally, in support of this objective and target, nine policy elements or priorities.
April 27, 1976

The national energy strategy for self-reliance presented in this paper is directed, through the next ten years, at minimizing the risks of growing dependence on imported oil. Self-reliance in energy means reducing our vulnerability to unanticipated changes in price or prolonged interruptions in supply. It means supplying Canadian requirements from Canadian resources to the greatest extent practicable, but it is not a strategy of self-sufficiency at any cost. It recognizes that we will have to rely on imported oil to a certain degree and an important policy element is emergency preparedness to ensure that Canadians using imported oil will be adequately protected if supplies should be curtailed.
Above all, it is a strategy that is both balanced and flexible: balanced in the sense that it recognizes that the policies we adopt will have costs as well as benefits, and a choice that provides the maximum advantage to Canadians must be found; flexible in the sense that many aspects of the international oil market and our own domestic energy situation are uncertain and continuing to evolve. The approach we have adopted will be dynamic enough to adapt quickly to changing circumstances.
The first target is to move domestic oil prices toward international levels, and to move domestic prices for natural gas to an appropriate competitive relationship with oil over the next two to four years. Domestic energy prices must continue to increase, to reinforce efficiency and restraint in energy use; to encourage the development of additional Canadian supplies; to reduce the magnitude of the transfer of real wealth from Canadians to oil exporting countries; and to reduce the subsidization of oil consumers by the general taxpayer. They need not move to international oil prices if it is clear that new Canadian resources can be found and delivered to markets at prices that are lower.
The second target is to reduce the average rate of growth of energy use in Canada over the next ten years to less than 3.5 per cent per year. This can be attained by appropriate pricing measures and energy conservation initiatives. It represents a reduction of the historically observed growth rate by over one-third.
The third target is to reduce our net dependence on imported oil in 1985 to one-third of our total oil demands, that is, to approximately 800,000 barrels a day by 1985.
The fourth target is to maintain our self-reliance in natural gas until such time as northern resources can be brought to market under acceptable conditions.
Finally, the fifth target is to double at a minimum, from $350 to $700 million a year, exploration and development activity in the frontier regions of Canada over the next three years, under acceptable social and environmental conditions. This is a minimum target that will facilitate the development of the information necessary to make appropriate decisions about our energy options.
In support of the objective of energy self-reliance, the government proposes nine major policy elements. These are; 1, appropriate energy pricing; 2, energy conservation; 3, increased exploration and development; 4, increased resource information; 5, interfuel substitution; 6, new delivery systems; 7, emergency preparedness; 8, increased
Energy Policy
research and development; 9, greater Canadian content and participation.
These policy areas are elaborated in the paper. In many cases specific examples of the kinds of programs and measures we will be introducing are indicated. For example, to further increase exploration and development we will be introducing a mandatory, company by company reporting system to monitor the cash flow of the petroleum industry. We will also move to reduce the period during which geophysical data remains confidential. To increase resource information flow we will be acting to require companies holding potentially important geological structures to have exploratory drilling undertaken within a reasonable time period. To promote new delivery systems for coal we are taking the position that before new export commitments are made producers should endeavour to determine whether a market exists within Canada for the additional coal production. Other specific measures such as conservation, research and development and greater Canadian participation that have recently been introduced or will be introduced shortly are described in the paper.
The precise nature of all future energy policy initiatives will continue to be determined within this framework but will, of course, be dependent on the course of future events. Such initiatives will embody the balance and flexibility that is essential if our policies are to be appropriate, and will reflect a changing relative emphasis among these nine policy areas as circumstances warrant. They will be developed with appropriate federal-provincial consultation and with due regard to the social, environmental and economic objectives of Canadians.
With the constructive co-operation of provincial governments and industry, and with the support of Canadians in all regions of the country, Canada can achieve the objective of energy self-reliance. Success in this endeavour will increase both the confidence and the options with which we can plan for years beyond 1985.

The government seems to have forgotten the constitutional principle that the resources of this nation belong to the provinces and decisions made in that respect must be made in consultation with them. That this document should come down without that sort of consultation is, indeed, too bad.
We are now also told to expect higher oil prices. Consultation with the provincial governments in respect of this important situation is not even mentioned in the document's blueprint for a phased increase toward international levels, and no assurance is given to Canadians that our prices will not exceed those of the United States, our biggest competitor. Surely the cornerstone of the development of our resources and the development of our energy policy in this country has to be established in the face of our enormous international trade deficit. If Canadian buyers and consumers of energy are not to face a comparative disadvantage because of present policies toward energy, then an assurance of this kind will have to be given.
Secondly, it is quite clear that the government has apparently decided to ignore the special energy problems faced by Atlantic Canada. In the immediate future, mari-timers can look forward to nothing but the hardship of escalating energy costs, in particular electricity prices which continue to mount and which will undoubtedly result in many more families being forced to find other ways to heat their homes. Nothing is planned to ease the burden of these costs, nor is there any federal assistance suggested to help in the generation of more electricity where the maritime provinces have some particular advantages. Nothing is said about the construction of a national grid, a policy which the Progressive Conservatives have advocated since 1969-indeed, since 1958. This matter must receive a great deal more support than this document suggests, if Atlantic Canada is ever to benefit and if ever such an energy grid is to become a reality in the nation.
Thirdly-and the minister said very little about this in his statement-the government has decided to press ahead with nuclear power as a major source of energy in this nation. The document cites a need to develop between
20,000	megawatt hours and 27,000 megawatt hours of new nuclear capacity within the next 15 years, a figure which is about equivalent to five reactors constructed every year. This is a massive commitment to an energy source which has attached to it many unanswered questions. How will we manage the highly toxic and radioactive wastes produced? How do we protect plants from natural and manmade disasters? Nothing is said about that. How are we going to protect ourselves against these disasters which can occur with the use of nuclear energy within our nation?
What is the competitive nature of this source of energy? A recent report prepared for the United States Energy Research and Development Administration showed that at current prices quoted for CANDU reactors, electric energy developed from the use of coal is competitive with nuclear power. Although the Canadian people are, by virtue of this document, committed to nuclear power, there is little discussion, especially in respect of the conclusions and the implications of this development. We simply cannot

embark upon this road without more thought and discussion.
The fourth decision is one which is implied throughout the document but never stated; that is, that the government has all but made the final decision to go ahead with Arctic oil and gas development. If the so-called policy of self-reliance upon which the document puts such emphasis is to be realized in the timetable set forth, it is apparent that Arctic gas must come on stream by the early 1980s. Even though the document states that no policy commitment yet exists, if the self-reliance policy is to succeed in reducing our projected oil imports to one-third of total demand, the Mackenzie Valley pipeline must surely become a reality. The question of whether or not we should have a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley has now become a question of when, not whether. The Berger Commission and the National Energy Board hearings, in light of this document, are not about whether a pipeline should be built but how it should be built and when it should be built. The decision has obviously been made.
There are a number of other features to this paper. The first is the government's virtual admission of ineptitude on a substantial scale in the budgets of 1974 and 1975. It is quite clear now that but for the prompt action of the Progressive Conservative government of Alberta, irreparable damage would have been done in respect of finding new supplies of gas and oil in Canada. It is to be hoped that when the new budget comes down the government will take into consideration the reflections in this report on its mistakes of the past, and we will then have a new and appropriate policy for oil and energy development in this country.
The government seems now to recognize the need for increased producer revenues. The minister has not outlined what specific measures he will take to ensure that this increased revenue will go back into exploration and development of energy in the future.
Finally, one can conclude that no matter how well or how badly conceived these policies may be, they have been put forward as a fait accompli without even the pretence of provincial consultation. Decisions have been made of fundamental importance without public hearing or debate. The minister has said in the past that his energy policies must become the policies of all Canadians, not just the government's. This document will not assure Canadians that that policy is being followed.

I ask the government to look at the catastrophic effect this will have on Canada's balance of payments and what position it will put us in with regard to our competitive status with American industry. The United States, by means of a blended price, has been able to keep the price of oil in that country $2 or $3 a barrel below the international price. Moreover, in the past few years we have witnessed, and may witness again, oil being used as a political weapon. By 1985, under this policy Canada would be very vulnerable both economically and politically.
What does the government propose to do about this as outlined in the report the minister tabled today? First of all, the minister said that the matter is mainly to be left to the private sector. He says that Petro-Can will have an important role, but he does not spell out what the role will be. As a matter of fact, this morning's paper carries a story by Mr. Maurice Strong, the chairman of Petro-Can, in which he says that that Crown corporation is seriously considering investing money overseas in the North Sea and in developing the oil sands of Venezuela. We have billions of barrels of oil in the Canadian oil sands, but our publicly-owned oil company is considering the possibility of developing the oil sands of Venezuela. Is that the role for which the Canadian people are putting up money?
The government proposes to deal with this situation by the old policy it has followed throughout the years, which I think is a disastrous policy. It proposes raising the domestic price to the international price within two to four years, which it is estimated will be $13 a barrel and perhaps higher. What guarantee does this House or the consumers of this country have that these additional millions of dollars we will pay to the oil industry will be plowed back into exploration and development in Canada rather than in the North Sea, Venezuela or the Middle East?
The minister says the government will monitor these companies to make sure that they use these additional earnings for exploration in this country. We were promised that by the minister's predecessor last year when the government raised the domestic price of oil from $6.50 to $8 a barrel. Has this monitoring taken place? What monitoring machinery does the government propose to set up?
Energy Policy
In the last three years the price of oil has gone from nearly $3 a barrel to $8 a barrel. If one looks at the record it will be evident that the money spent in exploration in Canada, as a percentage of the oil companies' earnings, has actually declined. The minister asks us to pay within the next two to four years $13 a barrel for oil and says that this money will be spent on finding oil and gas in this country. As a result, it is the Canadian consumer who buys the oil products-the Canadian taxpayer-because of the concession the government has so generously given the oil companies who will supply the funds for new exploration which will take place.
When the oil is found, the same people will buy it. This is known as a policy of pay now and pay again later. In the next ten years, the Canadian people will pay hundreds of millions of dollars in higher oil and gas prices in order to pay for the fact that this government for years allowed 60 per cent of our oil and gas to be exported to another country at prices only a quarter of what we will have to pay now for imported oil and domestic oil.
In this connection I want to say this is not a policy of reliance but it is a policy of drift. The tragedy is that once again the government is accepting the advice and acting on the recommendation of the very same powerful corporations which got us into this mess in the first place. The government is now proposing that we place our major reliance on pipelines into the Arctic and on nuclear power plants. In so far as pipelines into the north are concerned, the minister himself admitted that we do not have supplies or even proven reserves of oil or gas to justify the tremendous investment which will be necessary.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), in the statement he made yesterday in Yellowknife, said that unless we can prove up significant additional reserves we throw into very grave question the whole matter of the pipeline through the Mackenzie Valley. Some of us have been saying that for many years. The best estimate of the National Energy Board is four trillion cubic feet of gas reserves in the Mackenzie Delta. We require 12 trillion cubic feet as a minimum.
Why are we asking the Canadian people to approve an expenditure of $8 billion to $10 billion for a pipeline, the main function of which will be to transport Alaskan gas from Pudhoe Bay to the United States? The fact is that if we invest these tremendous sums of money in pipelines and in nuclear power plants, we will have nothing left with which to finance or to further develop alternate sources of energy. We are locking ourselves into two programs that will shut out what could be much cheaper sources of energy and in some cases would be less detrimental to the environment.
The government has not announced its policy with regard to looking at alternative energy sources. At page 145 of this report we are told that the government will spend, in 1975-76, $1.6 million and will spend in this current year $1 million in looking at such things as solar energy, wind energy, tidal power, and so on. That is a mere bagatelle. Other countries spend tremendous sums of money looking at these sources of energy. The government has done no realistic investigation into secondary recovery of oil. Mr. Speaker, a policy based on requirements is long overdue instead of a policy based exclusively on trade or consumer demand. Let me explain.
It is paradoxical today, when the minister is reporting on a relatively alarming energy situation, that we should-wonder whether there will be another energy shortage, especially as concerns oil and natural gas. The fact that Canada is still exporting daily hundreds of thousand barrels of oil or cubic feet of natural gas proves without a doubt, Mr. Speaker, the lack of foresight of a government that has failed to develop the required policy when it was needed.
We really should establish the energy requirements in Canada on the basis of our actual needs instead of foreign trade. I do not believe that in a country as vast as our ours, so full of all sorts of energy sources, with only 23 million inhabitants spread over a territory larger than the United States and larger than the whole of Europe, we should be talking about an energy shortage. It is only the mismanagement of governments that leads us to such an economic dead end in the field of energy. Indeed, how can we possibly have an oil shortage if we continue to export it? Mr. Speaker, the government should reply to such simple questions before sounding the alarm.
On a few occasions, I had the privilege in this House under Standing Order 43 of asking the government to make an inventory of the Canadian energy potential. Obviously, such an inventory would require the closest possible co-operation of the provinces, and I agree with the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the Conservative Party a while ago when he said that meaningful discussions and a coherent energy policy is not possible without the co-operation of the provinces. Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that Quebec has a great energy potential as concerns hydroelectric power. It seems to me that this energy, which has required an apparently substantial capital investment, which is easy to preserve and relatively unexpensive, may compensate for the oil shortage that might happen in eastern Canada. But there is no co-ordination, no planning whatsoever in this regard. Thus, some provinces have energy surpluses while others are at grips with shortages

and there is no co-ordination. The federal government should promote such co-ordination between all energy sources existing in the various regions of Canada. Of course, this cannot be done without extremely close co-operation.
Therefore, a precise inventory should be drawn up sometime. It should be kept up to date to enable us to know precisely what is available and what can be developed in Canada. We must no longer base our economy on those famous balances of trade with other countries or on exports. Let us simply ask ourselves, and this gives us the opportunity to do so, what we can do as Canadians. What are our energy requirements for the 23 million Canadians? Moreover, we must consider our energy potential. Mr. Speaker, once this has been seriously done, we will find out that we have all the energy required to meet our needs.
As long as the government refuse to see things as they really are, I suggest that we will always come to the point where we are told, as we were a few years ago, to turn down our thermostats, to shut the windows and not open too many doors. This is in my view a narrow policy, and it is time for the government to consider the introduction of a more serious, more positive policy, so that we know exactly where we are going.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-89, An act to amend the Anti-Inflation Act, be amended in clause 11 by striking out lines 10 to 23 at page 7 and substituting the following therefor:
"(2) This act expires on May 1, 1977, or on such earlier date as may be fixed by proclamation or a motion taken up and considered by the House of Commons that is adopted by the House and concurred in by the Senate pursuant to subsections (8) and (9) unless, before May 1, 1977, or any earlier date fixed by proclamation or any such motion that is so adopted by the House and concurred in by the Senate, an order in council is made to the effect that this act shall continue in force for such period of time as may be set out in the order in council."
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of my motion I would first like to say that I hope hon. members will participate at lenght in the debate with respect to this motion and also Bill C-89. I believe that one of the most important matters before this parliament is the question of the wage and price control program inflicted on the Canadian public by the government.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext: And supported by you on second reading.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
In that connection I would say that the minister's comment earlier today in the question period, that he hoped for speedy passage of this bill, was not unfortunate, bearing in mind that at committee stage with respect to the bill the guillotine was used once more by government members to force the bill through without proper review of the clauses therein. In short, we spent three meetings at committee stage reviewing this bill.
The same mistake was made by government members as was made respecting Bill C-73, the original anti-inflation legislation. That was giving too little time for thorough review at committee stage on this important matter which, unfortunately, ended up with amendments being required as we are now dealing with in Bill C-89. I say that because at the committee stage initially with respect to Bill C-73 it was made quite clear that we felt there were not proper appeal provisions under the legislation that the government was advancing.
My motion is, in effect, a very simple one. I suggest that we should deal with motions Nos. 1 and 2 jointly because they are interrelated. Motion No. 2 is consequential upon motion No. 1 being accepted. Motion No. 1 simply proposes to change the expiration date of Bill C-73 from December 31, 1978, to a more realistic date, namely, May 1, 1977.

speechtext:
If I may clarify that, Mr. Speaker, the bill we are dealing with today is Bill C-89, which in turn amends Bill C-73, but the expiration provision is in Bill C-73. What I am saying is that Bill C-73 contains the expiration date of December 31, 1978. The clause which is amended in another way by the administration is now being reamended through my motion to make the expiration May 1, 1977, as opposed to December 31, 1978.
April 27, 1976

I urge members of this House to support us in our desire to ensure that the wage and price control program of the present administration be held to a minimum period. It is our view that the honeymoon period with the Anti-Inflation Board appears to be on the wane. Six months after its creation, there is little evidence that the board has helped to contain inflation. Current moderation in inflation is due in the main to a decline since October in the prices of beef, pork, poultry, fresh fruits, cereal and bakery products. None of these items, however, come under the Anti-Inflation Board's direct purview, even in principle. Wage settlements reviewed by the board have ended in average first-year increases of 16.2 per cent, well above the board's target of 8 per cent plus 2 per cent for so-called productivity. More and more it appears that the present administration established the Anti-Inflation Board for political rather that economic reasons. Jean-Luc Pepin, chairman of the board, has apparently been asked to keep a high profile to give the impression of activity so that the administration can claim credit should inflation decline.
The present administration, in their anti-inflation program, appear-as far as the cabinet members and others are concerned-to be more and more as though they were TV actors playing out a script. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), I would suggest, takes the role of Marshall Dillon, out to vanquish the imagined villains, the labouring man, the businessman, the municipalities and the provinces. He, of course, has his little entourage. Festus, in the script, appears to be the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) limping along, meaning well but always fumbling and changing his mind. Jean-Luc Pepin, the board chairman, takes the role of Doc. His role is one of physician for all our problems. He is quick to prescribe aspirin remedies, but admits that he has no idea how to cure the overall disease of inflation. I am not sure who plays the role of Kitty in the program. It may be even Mrs. Plumptre, if you can imagine that.
As much as the administration may claim they are out to vanquish the villain of inflation, in the real world inflation always ends up vanquishing controls, if they are left on a permanent basis. The economies of western democracies are strewn with dead and wounded control programs that lasted too long. Controls only work on a temporary basis. Controls in themselves will not put an end to the inflation cycle. In fact, they may cause inflation to continue longer than they otherwise would. "Doc Pepin" will never put an end to the transfers of income and wealth that inflation brings. He will never be able to end the hardships inflicted by inflation on our poor and disadvantaged. Controls may be introduced appropriately as a supplementary or incidental device which for psychological reasons, at least, might assist the economy to right itself. Such controls must be subsidiary, however, to a tighter fiscal restraint and realistic growth in our monetary system.
It was on this basis that my party first suggested the imposition of an income control policy in Canada. We did that early in 1973. We based our proposition on the sound economic premise of having restraint in government spending and in the growth of our money supply. Had our approach of restraint in spending at the federal government level and in monetary growth been followed there is no doubt we could have shaved off the top of our inflation cycle and had less inflation today. Unfortunately, however,
Anti-Inflation Act
the present administration has subjected us to their control program for political reasons, not economic reasons. The administration is using this program to project an executive image of decisiveness in response to the public outcry to do something about inflation. In addition, they realize that the controls program shifts the focus of attention away from the real culprits of inflation-the government's own agency, the Bank of Canada, and the government's own spending-toward the private sector and the struggles between business and labour to maintain their income share.
The public relations' value is difficult to overestimate. Its ideal from the present administration's standpoint to have our commentators on TV and our columnists refer to labour or business leaders as being locked in confrontations against the public interest when they try to raise prices and wages. The administration's role then shows up as the protector, as the Marshall Dillon of the public interest rather than the culprit in the inflation process.
The electronic medium is perfectly suited to handle this shift in focus. Radio and TV people have a horrendous time depicting the complex process in which an undue increase in our money supply or federal spending creates inflation, but they have a very easy time depicting conflict between management and labour or consumer and supermarket. In this type of conflict the government always looks good. It is generally assumed they have no selfish interests, so they can appear to be the defender of the public and its protectors against selfish business and labour leaders. The Prime Minister and his officials wear white hats, carry halos and come on like Marshall Dillon with hundreds of deputized enforcers.
We were first told that the staff of the AIB would be 200 in number. At last count it was 583, and rising. After six months the number has reached nearly 600. Will it be 1,000 by the end of the year? At the highest point of the phase two control program in the United States the organization comparable to the AIB in Canada had only 700 people on its staff.
There is a growing indication that the government sees the control program in this country as a continuing one. Speaking in Toronto last weekend, the Minister of Finance told a meeting of Ontario Liberals that the wage and price control program might have to be tightened up so as to be more effective. He said that the program was, and I quote, "in a certain sense unjust to everyone", but that it had brought the rate of inflation down to about 9 per cent. Mr. Speaker, that is nothing but direct misrepresentation. There is no evidence that the program has materially reduced inflation. In fact, there is evidence to the contrary.
Let me cite two examples. I have already referred to the fact that the main reason for the decline in the rate of inflation is the drop in food prices. In the last three months, food costs declined to the equivalent of an annual rate of a 6.5 per cent increase, while the rest of the consumer price index package soared by 10.7 per cent. In the six months before the imposition of controls, the cost of living rose at an annual rate of 10.4 per cent. In other words, if you exclude the food component there is more inflation

April 27, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
today than existed prior to the commencement of the program.
My second example is this. Increasingly there is a tendency for wage settlements to be more generous than they might otherwise have been, since employers contemplate the AIB knocking down settlement levels anyway. There appears to be a shifting of responsibility from employers to the AIB in the blind assumption that the board will insist that its own guidelines should not be violated. However, we find that recent settlements approved by the board have on average been 50 per cent higher than permissible under the board's own guidelines.
Most alarmingly, there is increasing evidence that the government intends to continue the control program indefinitely, at least in part. Mr. Pepin speaks about the program having a gradual character and states, "It's only a dream if people start thinking of getting out of controls in 12 months or 18 months." The Minister of Finance has admitted to the committee that it is going to take a number of years to get inflation down to a level which in the government's view would justify dismantling the control program. The longer the controls continue, the more they will distort the economy. With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, I have moved, on behalf of the official opposition, that the anti-inflation program should expire on May 1 of next year rather than continue beyond that date.
Inflation in the United States is running this year at 6 per cent, compared to our own rate of 9 per cent. William Simons, Secretary of the U.S. Treasury, has forecast that inflation in that country will be down to 2 per cent in a couple of years. In Canada, on the other hand, the government talks about 8 per cent inflation this year, 6 per cent next year and 4 per cent thereafter-figures substantially above the American level.
The AIB has introduced a high degree of confusion into the marketplace. There is presently a backlog of 3,000 applications for price or wage review. According to the findings of a Gallup poll released last weekend, 67 per cent of those questioned thought the program was unfair with regard to prices, and 65 per cent felt it was unfair with regard to incomes. In the absence of public confidence there is little chance the board will be able to function effectively.
Speaking of confusion, in the course of the question period today I asked the minister at least to clarify the unfortunate inclusion of charitable donations under the restricted expense definition found in the Anti-Inflation Act regulations. His reply confirmed my worst impressions. Charitable donations, as an item included under restricted expenses, are now put into such a category that businessmen, acting in complete sincerity, may find it difficult to maintain their programs of charitable donations. I say this because what the minister has chosen to do by way of these regulations is to lump a large variety of expenses together under the heading of "restricted expenses." He has lumped advertising, promotion and public relations, plant and office rearrangement, moving, landscaping and decorating expenses, with expenses incurred in research and development, management fees, including administration fees, technical assistance charges and accounting service fees paid to any person with certain

exceptions. To all these things he has linked charitable donations and, finally, training and retraining expenses.
The unfortunate consequences are these. As a company carries on its business it may find that through no fault of its own advertising costs have increased. The cost of research and development might go up because the company feels it needs to spend more money in these areas in order to increase its productivity. Yet under the existing regulations the extra money needed will have to be found in one or other of the categories to which I have referred. For example, if a company wishes to increase its research and development program it might well feel it has no alternative but to lower its charitable donations in the current year. When we consider that more than 50 per cent of the money received by charitable organizations comes from business and commercial undertakings, I think it is particularly unfortunate that the regulations should be drafted in such a manner, the consequence of which might well be a substantial shortfall in donations to charitable donations such as the United Way in the current as well as subsequent years.
Initially, as I have pointed out, the administration stated that the board would have no more than 200 employees. As late as last November, Mr. Pepin is on record as saying, "The members of the board have a strong preference for a small agency, thus keeping the bureaucracy to a minimum." Last week, however, when appearing before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, he stated:
The original plan which called for a total of 200 officials was nonsense. It was simply a concept in the mind of one individual with no analysis of the situation at all.
It was then revealed that as of last month the board had built up a bureaucracy numbering 583 persons-and that figure is likely to be over the 600 mark by now. Besides the staff to which I have referred in the AIB itself, there is, of course, a staff in the administrator's office, in the office of the appeals tribunal and in other departments of government such as national revenue. In addition there is, of course, the provincial involvement. Speaking about staff, I think hon. members would be interested in an article that appears in the current, April edition of Executive magazine. It refers to the chaos existing at the AIB. The article has this to say:
Under the best of circumstances, the pace of expansion would have led to rather severe growing pains. But the differences among the board members and the lack of even minimal controls over the purse-strings have seriously compounded the problem. The growth has not been well orchestrated, internal co-ordination has been almost totally lacking, and personal empires are well under construction. In other words, the AIB's management is chaotic.
One sign of this is the high rate of turnover among the senior staff in almost every branch of the board.
Prices and profits: John Hague, the present director-general, is the second person to occupy the post. Hugh Bardon, his predecessor, walked out after a few weeks. But Hague himself is only temporary and he is expected to return soon to his regular job at the Canada Development Corp.
Compensation: James King already has returned to his consulting business in Toronto. He was succeeded by William Nelson as director-general at the start of March.
April 27, 1976

Communications: Michael McCabe resigned in February, being replaced as director-general on an acting basis by Kenn Prittie. A permanent replacement has yet to be appointed.
Administration: Ralph Blackwell, the present director-general, is the second person in the job.
Economic research: David Dodge is at least the second director-general; nobody can remember how many others have preceded him.
In that context, Mr. Speaker, can you blame the official opposition for saying that we should ensure that this unfortunate program should come to an end no later than May 1, 1977? The Americans, in their phase two program which ran from November 15, 1971, to January 11, 1973- about a 13-month period-took a much different approach from that which has been taken in Canada. Their program had three tiers of controls. The first tier, which involved 1,100 firms with $100 million or more in sales, covered 55 per cent of the gross sales in that country. Tier No. 2 covered another 1,500 firms which had sales of from $50 million to $100 million. This level caught 11 per cent of gross sales in the United States. The third tier, which applied to firms with sales under $50 million, involved only selected companies. In total, the United States did not attempt to control more than about 3,000 firms-a far cry from our approach.
In the American program, however, Mr. Speaker, they did attempt to control rents, with the result that 57 per cent of their field force was devoted to that field where they received 80 per cent of their complaints. We in Canada have passed rent control over to the provinces, yet our AIB staff is even larger than that in the United States if we look at the composite picture.
To date, the administration appears to have made three important mistakes in setting up their Anti-Inflation Board and the anti-inflation program itself. First, they did not provide for a total freeze during an initial 90-day period to allow for the forming of definitive rules which could be more easily understood. Secondly, they are allowing a highly discretionary approach to be taken in their decisions, with little consistency. Some wage and price decisions appear to be excessive, while others are unduly low. Thirdly, unlike the American approach, where about
3.000	firms were involved, the board has kept expanding their jurisdiction so that they are now reviewing over
100.000	concerns in this country. The workload and frustration that that will entail will become impossible. The administrative cost to businesses of complying with the controls will run into hundreds of millions of dollars.
In this connection, the United States has estimated that its control program may have reduced the rate of price and wage increases by no more than about 1 per cent, and that the main impact was at the beginning of their program. Against this one must consider the statement of John Dunlap, executive director of the cost of living council, when he appeared before the United States Senate committee on banking, housing and urban affairs on February 6,
1974.	At that time Mr. Dunlap had this to say:
One must consider the direct and indirect costs of the controls program. The direct costs consist of the administration necessary for the government and private sector to operate controls. The outlays of the federal government for implementing controls were $108 million for Phase II-
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the outlay for our program in Ottawa is running close to $20 million per year.
Anti-Inflation Act
Estimates on the administrative costs to business for complying with the controls regulation cover a range of from $0.7 to $2 billion, with the more realistic estimates at the lower end of the scale.
With 30 times the number of firms involved in Canada's control program already, the relative costs to Canadian companies may be truly staggering. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members should at least peruse the latest publication from the C.D. Howe Research Institute in a booklet "HRI Observations", which carries an article entitled "The Anti-Inflation Guidelines: Linking Wages to Productivity". I think this booklet sets forth some interesting perspectives and comments concerning this controls program, and on page 3 the following interesting statement is to be found:
-without an exceptional boost in productivity growth during the current recovery period, the guidelines will prolong the process of winding down the rate of inflation.
I think that the factual information given in this brochure should give everybody cause to be alarmed. Their view is that the 2 per cent productivity assumption that is built into the anti-inflation guidelines is not realistic in relation to productivity increases in this country. When the minister comments on my motion I should like to hear him deal with this question of productivity precisely.
Again on the question of confusion, I think it is interesting to note that not only did the government request the Anti-Inflation Board to comment on bringing various companies under the general regulation of the program-I am referring to the recent order in council directed at construction companies right down to the one-man company level, trucking companies, grain handling companies and shipping and longshoring establishments-but it has chosen to throw its net around the general insurance companies as well.
This is truly remarkable, Mr. Speaker. If you read the Anti-Inflation Board's recommendations regarding the inclusion of general insurance companies within the program, in effect the board stated that those that had automatically fallen within the guidelines-those with over 500 employees-did not dominate the industry sufficiently because there were so many other companies in the industry competing that the board could not effectively deal with that industry if the program were restricted to a relatively small number of companies.
The fact is that there are over 400 insurance companies doing business in Canada. What the government had failed to recognize is that the board was really basing its recommendation on the fact that they had found that most of those 400 companies were truly very competitive, and that unless they could control all insurance companies they felt they would be unable materially to alter the general carriage of business in the insurance industry of this country since the controls affected only a few of the big companies which, in percentage terms, represented only a small portion of the general insurance field. I would suggest that is a complete distortion. Reading it another way, the board should have said this is an industry that is truly competitive and does not need the control we are being asked to extend over it. To confirm this, I think it is interesting to note the statement by Mr. Humphrys, Superintendent of Insurance, before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs just this morning. I should like to quote what Mr. Humphrys said as follows:

April 27, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
The recent and current economic situation has strained companies' resources.
He was referring to companies active in the general insurance business. He continued:
Rising claims costs due to inflation and the resulting underwriting losses suffered have made it impossible to restore margins from retained earnings; at the same time the competition for capital and the poor profit performance have made it difficult to raise additional capital funds. This has caused some companies to withdraw from Canada and some others have had to impose restraints on the volume of new business.
Incidentally, on questioning Mr. Humphrys he stated that 27 companies to date have had to withdraw from Canada because the insurance business is so competitive they no longer felt they could continue to make money here carrying on with the general insurance business. Mr. Humphrys went on to state:
The situation has required, and is requiring, sustained attention by the department to see that unsatisfactory asset positions and operating losses are recognized and corrected within time limits imposed, in order to ensure that companies remain in a position where they are able to discharge their financial obligations to the public. We are re-examining the statutory requirements for reserves and surplus margins to be sure that they do not unnecessarily impede companies in providing insurance that the public needs.
Those are alarming words coming from the Superintendent of Insurance. He is stating that the losses sustained by these companies were something over $200 million in 1974, and almost $200 million in 1975, have resulted in these companies being extremely strained as far as their capital resources are concerned. To suggest that they be subjected to still more harassing control and regulation shows the ineptitude of the government's handling of this entire anti-inflation program.

My friends to the left, in typical fashion, hoot and holler when I refer to the insurance industry. subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS PROVISION FOR ABATEMENT OF NOISE LEVELS IN FACTORIES
HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS PROVISION FOR ABATEMENT OF NOISE LEVELS IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-247, an act respecting noise in factories, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as spelled out in the explanatory note attached to it, is to combat a major health hazard in industry by requiring that the
April 27, 1976

noise levels in establishments having contracts with the government of Canada shall be a maximum of 85 decibels. The noise volume at 85 decibels is said by health experts to be "when you can hardly hear yourself talk".
Noise control has been a very complicated and controversial issue due to the complex nature of noise itself and its effects. Noise has been defined as any sound that is regarded or treated as a nuisance. But the degree of annoyance is not necessarily related to the intensity of sound. What may be music to one person is noise to another. Certainly, attitude of mind and environment are of major importance. This factor and others further complicate the debate raging on the best means of measuring noise, the most effective and feasible manner of protecting workers and the health effects of noise.
I have neither the expertise nor the inclination to become involved in that kind of discussion which brings in countless variables and employs scientific and technical jargon. I believe that kind of debate is too often used to slow down or halt noise abatement efforts rather than seriously attempting to find ways of controlling unwanted and excessive sounds. This "talk but don't act" mentality has resulted in slower progress in changing the law than technology's capacity to make more noise.
There can be no question of a man's right to work in an environment which will not harm him, and there is no doubt that noise which is loud enough and consistent enough will harm him. The degree of this harm and the scope of the health effects caused by noise-for which a wide variety of physiological and psychological effects have been postulated-is at present uncertain. However, one area where there is unanimous agreement is that noise can, and does, cause hearing loss whether it is temporary hearing loss or permanent hearing loss, or permanent injury to the inner ear. These effects are an established fact of living and working in an industrial society; there is no controversy over this point.
Another point that is not very controversial is how hearing loss occurs. The most common kind of industrial hearing problem develops when the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, which transmit sound pressure along nerves to the brain, are damaged. Exposure to high noise levels can cause these cells to become fatigued, resulting in temporary loss of hearing ability. The ear can usually recover, once the noise is removed, in a period ranging from minutes to days. However, if the noise is loud enough and long enough over months or years, the cells are destroyed and the damage is permanent.
At what level, then, does hearing loss begin? This point varies widely with individuals and it is often difficult to separate work-induced hearing loss from contributing noise factors off the job. However, in the summer of 1975 the U.S. occupational safety and health administration held 41/2 weeks of hearings which included 139 presentations of testimony. During the hearings the occupational safety and health administration presented estimates based on a sample of 19 major U.S. industries employing about 14.5 million workers. With this group it was found that a strictly enforced-I repeat, strictly enforced- 90-decibel limit of noise for an eight-hour work day would keep 463,000 workers, or 3.2 per cent of the work force, from suffering hearing loss after 40 years of exposure, still
Noise in Factories
leaving 130,000 at risk of hearing impairment. Lowering that limit to 85 decibels, according to OSHA, would prevent hearing loss for another 73,000 workers, or 0.5 per cent of the work force. The U.S. national institute for occupational safety and health estimate that as many as 10 per cent to 15 per cent more workers might suffer hearing loss if exposed to 90 decibels, instead of 85 decibels, over a working lifetime.
As I stated earlier, health problems may not be the only result of high noise levels. A number of experts have suggested that by acting on the nervous system, noise increases the pulse rate and may raise the chances of high blood pressure and the occurrence of stress, which could have measurable effects. However, while many noise abatement proposals mentioned non-auditory effects of noise, most are aimed only at preventing hearing loss since research on these other possible effects is still inconclusive.
Although Canada does not have specific legislation dealing with noise control in industry at either the federal or provincial level, there are protective legislative provisions at both levels of government as part of other statutes. Federal legislation for noise control, found under the Canada Labour Code as the Canada noise control regulations, exist as statutory orders and regulations. The regulations affect noise control and hearing conservation in federal works undertakings and businesses. The regulations state that where reasonably practicable, employers must not permit employees to work where the sound level is 90 decibels or more. Otherwise, permissible noise exposure is scaled from eight hours per work day at more than 87, but not more than 90 decibels, to zero hours at more than 115 decibels. A worker may be permitted exposure to 90 decibels or more where a suitable hearing protector is worn which reduces the sound level to less than 90 decibels, or where a hearing test establishes no hearing impairment for employees exposed to 90 to 95 decibels and regular tests are made.
The United States has a 90-decibels standard for an eight-hour work day, similar to that adopted under the Canada Labour Code and by several provinces. However, the currently developing goal in the United States for maximum industrial noise exposure is 85 decibels for an eight-hour work day. This standard is being considered for adoption by the occupational safety and health administration in Washington. It would appear that this level might very possibly be adopted, at least as a goal for the near future. In addition, the Soviet Union, Australia, Czechoslovakia, Finland, Sweden, East and West Germany, and South Africa have adopted the 85-decibel industrial noise limit.
It is clear that industrial noise control in Canada lags seriously behind that of a number of other countries, including the United States. The cost of inadequate noise control is high, not only in terms of health damage but also in the context of compensation payments. For example, between 1971 and 1974 the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario paid out more than $2.5 million to people who had significant hearing loss from noise damage. It appears, as Robert Baron says in his book "The Tyranny of Noise", that-

April 27, 1976
Noise in Factories
Society seems to look upon any degree of excessive noise as it now regards pornography-if it contains a modicum of social value, it is not obscene.
However, perhaps it is somewhat unfair to blame all of society for the lack of effective controls on noise pollution, for the bulk of the blame must lie with governments and corporations. Too often, noise abatement is presented not as an essential but as a luxury. But who considers the ability to hear a luxury? We have to stop weighing economic considerations against public health and welfare. Indeed, it sometimes appears that more emphasis is placed on reducing noise complaints instead of noise.
As I indicated earlier, there is considerable debate about the present noise limit of 90 decibels for an eight-hour work day versus the proposed 85 decibels limit. In the United States, a number of organizations including the environmental protection agency and the national institute for occupational safety and health are supporting the adoption of the 85 decibels limit. Most major labour unions are also supporting this standard. Industry, by and large, is opposed to the establishment of the 85-decibel standard, especially in older plants, on the understandable grounds that the program will be prohibitively expensive. Industry's spokesmen argue, instead, for the use of hearing protection devices such as ear-plugs and ear-muffs. Labour groups argue against the use of these devices on the grounds that they are often improperly worn and thus give insufficient protection. In other cases, because the devices are hot and uncomfortable over long periods, workers frequently refuse to wear them at all unless they are directly supervised.
It may seem much more practical to have workers wear ear-plugs or ear-muffs rather than spending millions of dollars to convert machinery so that it meets the minimum noise standards. While in the short run this may be the only alternative, I believe industry must begin to place emphasis on designing machinery which will be much quieter. I really do not believe industry will take this initiative until it is forced to do so. Corporations have always argued against pollution controls-and let us make no mistake that noise is a form of pollution-on the ground that such controls were economically not feasible. However, environmental studies have generally shown that without such controls the cost will be much higher. In an article by George Clack entitled "The Noise Control Controversy" he refers to a recent long-range study which shows the same is true for noise controls. He said:
Dr. Nicholas Ashford, from the center for policy alternatives at MIT, analysed the costs and benefits of compliance over various periods of time for both 90 decibels and 85 decibels limits. By placing a dollar value on the benefits of less worker's compensation, absenteeism, and mental annoyance, he discovered that after 40 years an 85 decibels limit would actually be cheaper than a 90 decibels limit.
In conclusion, I hope hon. members will see fit to send Bill C-247 to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for further study or, at the very least, the subject matter of this bill. If we fail to take some action on this matter, we may very well be condemning an untold number of workers to partial or complete deafness.

subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS PROVISION FOR ABATEMENT OF NOISE LEVELS IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Toronto-Lake-

shore (Mr. Robinson) on the introduction of this bill which, if passed, would be entitled "An act respecting noise in factories". The hon. member has made a good case for a proposition which we all support, namely, that in too many places there is too much noise pollution. One might say that at times it is not only in work places. I have seen places of entertainment and I have dropped in on parties which have taken place on this hill around the middle of December where I am sure the noise level was much higher than 85 decibels. There may be times during the question period in the House of Commons when the level gets fairly high as well.
At any rate, to be serious, I think the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore has done a service in bringing this subject before the House and I hope the House will be willing in this private members' hour to agree to this bill and send it to the standing committee. I think it is appropriate that it should go to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration because it does relate to noise in work places.
If I have some misgivings about the bill, they relate to the narrowness of its application and to the lack of any provisions for its enforcement. I remind the House that we already have in the Canada Labour Code a part which deals with safety. Back in earlier days we had two or three separate federal labour codes and one of them dealt entirely with safety. That particular act has now been incorporated into the Canada Labour Code as a whole and it lays down conditions with respect to the atmosphere, temperature, noise and any conditions which affect the health of our workers. I can say from some experience that when that legislation was first brought before this House a number of years ago we were urged to get it through in a hurry because the Department of Labour wanted to get moving on it, and despite that, these many years later there are still factories in this country where there are health hazards of various kinds because the Department of Labour has found it difficult to enforce the provisions of that act.
But this particular bill which is now before us does not provide for any enforcement provisions at all. It is limited in that it refers only to those factories which get federal government contracts, and I think we should go much further. That is not to be taken as a stand against the bill. I think the idea in it is a commendable one and I want to see the bill go to committee. However, I hope that in committee we might find ways of incorporating this into the Canada Labour Code so that the attempt to avoid noise pollution will be made not just in those factories which get government contracts but in all work places which come under federal labour jurisdiction.
I was critical a few moments ago with respect to the tardiness of the Department of Labour in putting into effect the provisions regarding safety which are in the Canada Labour Code. On the other hand, I know that genuine efforts have been made by the federal Department of Labour in co-operation with the various provincial departments of labour to get safety accepted and practised in all work places. I have the feeling that this little bill, standing by itself with no provisions for enforcement, will not do the job. What we need to do is put into the Canada Labour Code itself these provisions regarding 85 decibels
April 27, 1976

over an eight-hour period, being all workers should be asked to experience, and I hope that if we could get it into the labour code with provisions for enforcement, the excellent proposals of the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore could be implemented.
So I commend my hon. friend across the way for bringing in another useful bill. He will be running up something of a record if he gets this bill through today. He got one through a short while ago. All power to him. We on this side of the House do not have that experience very often. However, it is high time we did something about noise pollution in Canada in all kinds of places. Because this is a small beginning in that direction, we are glad to give our support to Bill C-247.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS PROVISION FOR ABATEMENT OF NOISE LEVELS IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the preceding two speakers and to say in a few words how this bill relates to the federal Department of the Environment. Under the Government Organization Act, 1970, the Minister of the Environment is charged with the responsibility to initiate, recommend and undertake programs and co-ordinate programs of the government of Canada which are designed to promote the establishment or adoption of objectives or standards relating to environmental quality, or to control pollution and promote and encourage the institution of practices and conduct leading to better protection and enhancement of environmental quality.
Consistent with this mandate, between November, 1972, and January, 1973, departmental staff conducted a series of bilateral meetings with all provinces on the subject of environmental noise control. These meetings led to arrangement of a conference of federal and provincial officials in Ottawa on May 1, 2 and 3 of 1973. With the exception of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, all the provinces were represented. At the federal, level, the Department of the Environment, the Ministry of Transport, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Privy Council Office were represented. The provincial representatives were unanimous in requesting the permanent establishment of a federal-provincial committee on noise to act as a forum for the exchange of technical and other information on noise and to assist in the development of proposals to improve the collective capability to manage noise problems in Canada.
At the meeting of federal and provincial ministers of the environment on May 8 and 9, 1973, several provincial ministers strongly endorsed the formalization of the federal-provincial committee on noise. Formal appointments to the committee were made during the summer of 1973 and the first meeting was convened in April, 1974. Two technical subcommittees have been formed, one dealing with general aspects of community noise and the other with specific noise sources.
We consider such federal-provincial interaction to be essential in developing an effective and nationally integrated approach to noise control, particularly since we are dealing in an area of mixed or overlapping jurisdiction. We believe that our program proposal provides for an effective
Noise in Factories
approach to promoting and stimulating efforts in this area and in bringing together the various agencies, both federal and provincial, having responsibility and authority to effect the desired control measures.
Of course, Environment Canada's primary interest in the noise control field is directed to what may be termed "environmental noise". Environmental noise may be considered as noise which may be perceived over a relatively wide area and is harmful or disturbing to individuals or to local ecosystems. Bill C-247, on the other hand, appears to be directed to the control of "occupational noise". Environment Canada's interest, then, is somewhat peripheral, recognizing that occupational health and safety are a more direct responsibility of the departments of labour and national health and welfare and that provincial jurisdiction is also involved. However, it must also be recognized that reduced noise exposure levels in the work place may in some instances also result in reductions in noise in the environment surrounding a particular industrial activity.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on, but I shall not, to describe many other activities of the Department of the Environment and the requirements and procedures that have to be followed and that are established relative to noise pollution specifically. I could talk about the environmental protection agency and all that, but I shall conclude my remarks simply in an effort to accommodate the hon. gentleman who introduced this bill because I am in perfect agreement with the general thrust of the bill itself. Therefore, I shall not prolong the debate. I will simply say that it should be noted that much of the legislative jurisdiction over occupational noise rests with the provinces. That is going to be a problem.
Bill C-247 proposes limits for noise in industrial establishments working on government contracts. Noise control of the type considered could be introduced through requirements written into the contracts rather than through a new federal act. It is specified in clause 3 of the bill that subject to section 4, noise levels shall not exceed 85 decibels. There are various types of decibel representation of sound and the type of decibel should be clearly indicated in a noise specification of this type. Also, the effects of noise depend, among other things, on the duration of exposure to the noise. A proposed noise limit such as this one should indicate the duration of the noise exposure, as is done, for instance, in the Canada noise control regulations of the Canada Labour Code. It may have been intended that the decibels in clause 3 of the bill be A-weighted. A short exposure to 85 A-weighted decibels of noise would not have deleterious effects on human beings, and in fact such short exposures often occur in harmless occupational and non-occupational situations.
Officials of the Department of the Environment will continue to work toward the implementation of an effective national program in environmental noise control, and will work in close co-operation with officials of the Department of Labour and the Department of National Health and Welfare in overlapping areas of interest related to occupational noise and to the direct and indirect effects of noise exposure on human health.
