subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before five o'clock I had referred to the very obvious difference of opinion between the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) on the one hand, who is critical of the Anti-Inflation Board because it exercised its judgment, to quote his phrase, in a highly discretionary way with little consistency-those are his words-with respect to the historical relationship of certain of the collective bargaining units that had come before its attention, and the viewpoint expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) earlier today not because the Board had not exceeded the guidelines, but had not exceeded them by enough. They felt the Anti-Inflation Board had not gone far enough beyond the guidelines.
I think the answer was given by himself, although he obviously did not understand it, to the hon. member for Vancouver South in the very question he asked, in which he said, "But what if you are not to allow it to Thompson, are you not going to allow it to Snow Lake, Lynn Lake and a number of other mining communities in northern Manitoba?" That is the exact point. If one has to repeat it again and again throughout the work force, where is the restraint? Where are we going to have restraint on incomes in the work force? If you have a continual pyramiding of labour costs in our community, let us not kid ourselves, people will have to pay for it and it will add to the level of inflation in Canada.
His question involved another contradiction. Again the hon. member for Vancouver South obviously did not understand it. He said he was concerned about the work force leaving Thompson and going somewhere else. Where else-Snow Lake, Lynn Lake, or the other communities? If all those communities are restrained in the same way, to what avail is it to leave one for the other? That is the exact point of applying a general system of this kind to restrain incomes throughout the community.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe made some reference to the American anti-inflation program. He has come back
April 27, 1976

from there and apparently is an expert on this question. I think it is fair to point out to him that that program was in effect for nearly three years, August 1971 to April 1974. It included a whole range of remedies, including not one but two freezes, and various kinds of selective controls in that period of time. Therefore there is obviously no single answer involved in how to bring about an effective mandatory controls program of this kind except to point out that, whatever one may say about the American experience, it lasted generally as long as the period of time contemplated under this particular program.
The hon. member made some reference to the fact that there are 100,000 firms now covered by the provisions of the controls. Perhaps he was being a little disingenuous in that. He referred to the fact that the vast majority of firms had been added as a result of the judgments of the AntiInflation Board with regard to association bargaining situations, the situation where a group of employers and firms are associated to bargain as a group with a group of employees, with a collective bargaining representative on their side.
The important fact to bear in mind is that those involved in this association bargaining process, firms, and in many cases the employees themselves, wanted the anti-inflation program to be extended to them as well so that it would not break up what in their viewpoint had been regarded as an advantageous way of dealing with labour relations. Therefore when the hon. member refers to 100,000 firms, he is obviously exaggerating. To be more honest, he should refer to about 143 associations which bargain collectively with their employees for the purpose of determining their wage levels.
The final point he made was with regard to his question during the Question Period about charitable donations. As I pointed out at that time, the government has indicated a certain level of restricted expenses so as to get around the situation where a firm could decide to increase its prices, with the consequent cost which would have to be borne by the consumer, and at the same time escape the profit restrictions of the anti-inflation program for the years of the application of the program by increasing its expenses a certain amount. This could be done, for example, by advertising promotion, expenditure on research and development, charitable donations, and action in a number of other areas. Clearly, restraint provisions inherent in the profit controls under the anti-inflation program would not be effective in holding prices down if firms could increase their prices and escape the profit control by that kind of practice. It is for that reason the guidelines provide that the over-all category of these restricted expenses may not be increased in any one year at any greater rate than the increase in the total returns to the firm.
The hon. member laid some store on the argument that it was regrettable that charitable contributions or expenses incurred on research and development might be reduced. Well, I suppose that if a firm were to decide to cut down its charitable contributions and increase its advertising promotion or its expenses on public relations, or if it wanted to increase its expenses on landscaping or decorating, which is another area of restricted expenses, or its expenses in connection with conventions for so-called edu-
Anti-Inflation Act
cational purposes, it could do so. But let it not do so with a high moral tone pretending that the anti-inflation program was curtailing it in that regard. It is the firm's own priorities which determines whether money is put into landscaping, for example, rather than into charitable contributions. Hon. members should bear in mind that if a firm feels constrained to curtail charitable donations because it has to increase expenditures in other areas, this is an indication of the firm's own priorities.
The bill before us will extend the benefits of the appeal provisions to certain people affected by decisions of the Anti-Inflation Board and will provide certain additional legal measures to make the present anti-inflation program more effective. This measure has been outstanding for some time now, during which period the rights of appeal of certain groups have been abridged. I will terminate my remarks at this stage in the hope that we may secure early passage of the legislation in order that those rights might be available to persons affected by the Board's decisions.

speechtext:
At the
outset, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate the New Democratic Party's support for the bill before us. I do so at least in part for the reason that we can claim to have had something to do with the origin of the bill in the first place.
The House will recall that about two months ago, as a result of the settlement in the Irving case, we moved a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 26 calling for an emergency debate on precisely this issue, the case of workers in Canada not having any right of appeal at all. Certainly they had no effective right under the existing legislation. An emergency debate was permitted by Mr. Speaker at that time. Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the amendments to the bill which are before us. But before doing so I must say I have never listened in all my life to such a contradictory speech as that presented today by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who used his full 40 minutes castigating the whole antiinflation program. There was nothing good about it, in his view.
The hon. member listed objections which have arisen because of the lack of efficacy of the price control program; he listed objections based on inequities in terms of the effects on wages and salaries of Canadians from coast to coast; he complained about the effect on the corporate sector. In short, he said nothing good about the whole measure. He then presented an amendment which would have the effect of extending the life of the bill, permitting this measure to remain as part of the law of Canada, for fully another year. I would presume, Mr. Speaker, that only a member of the Conservative party could adopt such a contradictory position on a measure of this nature. He cannot have it both ways. Either the anti-inflation program embodied in the law of Canada at the present time is on balance a good program and acceptable to a party or to a member of the House of Commons and is therefore supportable or, on balance, the program is bad for whatever variety of reasons, in which case a logical mind or logical part would reject it.
I repeat, the spokesman for the Conservative party rose in his seat and spoke for 40 minutes against the bill, then made a proposal which would lead to its maintenance on

April 27, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
the law books of Canada for fully another year. If any speech was attempting to have things both ways, then surely the one we heard from the hon. member was doing so. I hear an hon. member to my right protesting; he is shaking his head and presumably he agrees with the hon. member for York-Simcoe. He asks, "why not have it for a year?" I say to him that if a kick in the head is bad twice, it is no reason for him to accept being kicked in the head once. The Conservative member again insists that it is good to have one kick in the head. Well, that may be true for the Conservative Party of Canada, Mr. Speaker, but it is not true for the New Democratic Party. We said when this measure was first announced last Thanksgiving, that it was bad in principle. We said so when the bill was introduced shortly afterward, and we say so again tonight. What is bad for two, three or four years is, for us, equally bad for one year. You cannot have it both ways.
Because I intend to move a sub-amendment which I hope will be consistent with what I have to say, and one which goes to the principle of the legislation which is embodied in the proposal put before us by the hon. member for York-Simcoe, I want to say something very briefly about the existing legislation and its effects on the people of Canada.
It is, I think, worth noting, that the Gallup poll seeking the opinion of the people of Canada on this legislation recently revealed the conclusion that 65 per cent of Canadians think the program is unfair in terms of wages and salaries. Second, 67 per cent of Canadians think the program is unfair in terms of its effect on prices in Canada. This may well have been the reason why the hon. member for York-Simcoe made the kind of speech he did. He is now catching up to the people of Canada. They are feeling its effects. If they were here tonight they would obviously be voting against it. Certainly they would not commit the absurdity of speaking for 40 minutes against a measure and then, in effect, voting for its continuance.
The people of Canada now realize the program is unfair in its impact on wages and salaries. The rulings of the board in this area have been remarkable for their inconsistency. One has only to name a few categories of workers in highly disparate occupations and the facts speak out to support my statements. We think of the librarians in Toronto, and of the miners in Thompson. Just in the last few days we have been talking about the miners. The minister a few minutes ago scoffed at the suggestion that the workers in Thompson might leave Thompson because of the grossly unfair wage settlement which was imposed by the Board. The Minister of Finance asked, "Where are are they going to go?" He listed a whole number of places to which they might move and implied they weren't going anywhere.
Just for the minister's information, in case he is not aware of them, here are some figures with respect to the rate of labour mobility in Thompson, Manitoba, in the very company affected by the decision. In 1970 that company had a 124 per cent turnover in its labour force, in 1971 it was 112 per cent, in 1972 it was 101 per cent, in 1973 it was 84 per cent, in 1974 it was 130 per cent, and in 1975 it was 118 per cent. These figures are significant. They illustrate that Thompson is an isolated community, one to which most working people do not readily go. One of the major

reasons for considering a move to that difficult northern environment is that at least the wage or salary offered will afford some kind of compensation for such a move.
I also want to put on the record the comparison with other workers in the same industry who live in Sudbury, Ontario. These workers are getting a higher rate of pay. It is with this group of workers that the Thompson workers should have been compared for historical reasons, and the board should have reached the same settlement and given them the same rate of pay. There is not the same isolation problem in Sudbury. Workers in that community in 1975 had a labour turnover of only 6.7 per cent. Compare that with the turnover in Thompson, Manitoba, for the same year of 118 per cent. Surely even the Minister of Finance can see the significance of these two different sets of figures. In the one case it is unpleasant and difficult to work in terms of accessibility to other populations living in reasonable climatic conditions; in the other case such problems do not exist.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if that AIB had an ounce of intelligence in terms of dealing equitably with this group of workers, it would have assured that in its decision of recent days the Thompson workers in Manitoba would have been given an increase fully commensurate with and equal to the remuneration received by their fellow workers in Sudbury who are doing the same kind of job. That is only one glaring and unfortunate illustration of the kind of inequitable decisions we have been getting from the AntiInflation Board.
Another vivid example is a decision announced the same day affecting the uranium workers in the Elliott Lake region of Ontario. These workers are susceptible to cancer and silicosis to a degree way out of proportion to almost every other category of worker in Canada. There is every reason to believe, now that it is common knowledge among the people of Canada, as it should have been a long time ago, that the pension plan that was negotiated by the steelworkers union in Elliot Lake on behalf of its workers, as part of the package considered by the AIB, was an essential feature so far as the work force was concerned. This was a provision for early retirement for the workers in the uranium industry. To put it bluntly, Mr. Speaker, early retirement is essential to many of these workers if they are to avoid getting cancer or silicosis.
Be that as it may, in making its ruling on the package settlement for the workers in the uranium industry the Anti-Inflation Board did not consider this fact, even though it knew full well that in considering financial benefits one includes pension plans as well as hourly pay rates. If the board gives a much lower settlement than is fair and equitable, inevitably it will mean that the pension plan will be affected and that workers in those circumstances will suffer a deterioration in their health, resulting-and I say this bluntly-in premature death for a number of them. This illustrates how serious is the AntiInflation Board's decision, yet the government had done nothing about it, saying benignly that it will leave it to the board and hope for the best.
I am not going to take the time to go over the whole range of decisions that have been made in past months; I
April 27, 1976

cite here but two glaring and unfortunate examples. The general point that I want to make is that at the outset of this program, in view of the way it is set up and in view of the legislative provisions, the New Democratic Party said that the people who would be most seriously and adversely affected by it would be the working Canadians, the ordinary people on wages and salaries, the majority of whom are not even members of a trade union, like the steelworkers who at least are able to go to bat and fight against the board, as in the case of the unfair decisions affecting the workers in Thompson and Elliot Lake. Most ordinary Canadians do not even have a union to do this kind of work for them.
There are now over 5,000 decisions which have to be made by the board. In the meantime hundreds of thousands of workers across Canada are waiting for a decision to see how their income and livelihood will be affected. A more monstrous bureaucracy one can hardly imagine, Mr. Speaker.
What about prices? The whole thrust of the program was geared toward bringing down prices in Canada, but what is the record after the legislation has been on the law books of Canada for six months? The fact is that the very prices the board was set up to control or bring down have gone up. Discounting the effect of food prices from the recent cost of living figures which were published in the past two weeks, which you must, Mr. Speaker, because the program does not control prices of food at the farm gate, you will discover that the very items the board was set up to control have led at this point in our history to a greater increase in the rate of inflation than the increase last year when we had no such program. Could a more damning comment than that be made about the efficacy of this program? The fact is that the very items this program was set up to control, those that affect the cost of living, are now increasing at a more rapid rate than they were in 1975.
The only prices ordered rolled back in the more than six months of existence of the board have been the price of beer sold by one brewer in the province of Quebec, and secondly-and this one almost brought tears to my eyes- Imperial Oil, that poor petroleum corporation, was not allowed to increase the price of a gallon of gasoline recently by IVi cents but was only permitted an increase of one cent a gallon by the board. That was really touching.
The reality of the situation is that the government is committed in principle to allowing this same petroleum corporation, Esso, and all the others, to increase the price of oil at the wellhead up to the world price level. Within the next two weeks there will be an announcement by the government that oil companies in Canada will be able to increase their prices by $1.50 to $2 a barrel, I predict, and this increase will be passed on to the consumer. As a result poor old Esso, which got an increase of only one cent of a gallon in the recent decision of the AIB, will be permitted within a couple of weeks to increase more than a hundred fold the price of oil which every consumer will pay for, whether he pays for it by driving his car, heating his home, or by buying products made by industries that are dependent upon oil for their energy.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, in more than six months of existence only two price rollbacks have been ordered by the AIB. One rollback was in the price of beer in the
Anti-Inflation Act
province of Quebec, and the second was a half cent reduction in the increase in the price of oil by the Esso Corporation.
I noted with interest, that Mr. Pepin, the Chairman of the AIB, recently said that we could expect an escalation in prices during the latter half of 1976. The reason, he said, is that the corporations will by that time understand the law and its complexities much better than they do now. Is that not again moving? They are going to come to a better understanding of the law of Canada during the next few months, and therefore they will be more able to increase prices, and more able in many if not all cases to gouge the people of Canada because their lawyers and accountants will have a more thorough grasp of the legislation that is on the books! The forecast then is that the situation is going to get worse and not better in terms of prices for Canadians.
I have simply reiterated our opposition to the legislation. It was unfair and unworkable when it was brought forward in the fall. It has turned out to be unfair and unworkable ever since it has been on the books. It is something the Canadian population, in terms of the most recent Gallup poll, has seen to be unfair and unworkable. It is not something we in this party can put up with any longer. Therefore I should like to move an amendment to the motion we are debating, as follows:
That Motion No. 1 be amended in line 1 of the proposed new subclause (2) by changing "1977" to "1976" and by deleting all the words thereafter.
This amendment is seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
Just before I sit down let me say I have no hope at all of the government ever changing its mind. A Liberal never does that unless he is going to lose a vote over something. I do appeal to the Conservative party for once in its history to show consistency. I urge in particular the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) to re-read his speech and follow the logical conclusion. If he reads his speech and reaches the logical conclusion he will end up favouring this amendment, because if it passes it would mean at the end of this week, symbolically on May Day, this unfair and unworkable law presently with us in Canada would be no longer in existence.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO ADD NEW DEFINITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of the motions but down by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) I propose to address my remarks to the manner in which the AntiInflation Board has managed to become a bureaucracy of confusion, not only to those whom it attempts to regulate, but also to itself. This unfortunate situation is not surprising to many of us, especially in light of the circumstances surrounding the creation of the board.
In July, 1974, the present government, while allowing the Canadian economy to deteriorate to a position where drastic action was required, won itself an election by grandly denying that an economic problem existed. Leading up to that federal election we had a minority government and Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was forced to go to the polls by the opposition. The major issue was inflation, and the major proposal put forward by the then Leader of the

April 27, 1976
Anti-Inflation Act
Opposition was a 90-day freeze followed by selective temporary wage and price controls, and coupled with major economic policy initiatives designed to attack the root causes of our economic problems.
The Prime Minister was at his best, however, as he forayed back and forth across the country attacking, belittling, and ridiculing. Again and again he used the same catch words about these controls-hocus-pocus, baloney, and simplistic. He told the voters controls would never work. They failed in the United States and Britain, he said. You cannot control food prices, interest rates, housing costs, energy prices, dividends or the cost of imports. The only controllable area is that of wages, he told the people, and no self-respecting Canadian wants to see that.
As a result of this performance the Prime Minister returned to office with a majority and a mandate to refuse the imposition of controls. A scant 15 months later the Prime Minister came full circle and informed Canadians that his program of wage and price controls was the cure to the country's economic ills, economic ills which the Prime Minister found impossible to continue ignoring.
It was at this stage that the Anti-Inflation Board was created to regulate the economy single-handedly and slay the dragon of inflation. This Anti-Inflation Board was denied the advantage that a 90-day freeze had offered, and it was thrown into the task at hand to the sounds of confrontation from both labour and business as the Prime Minister threatened the nation with imprisonment for failure to comply with his ill-conceived and hastily prepared program. With a birth like that it is a wonder the board has even survived. That birth, again considering the haste with which the program was formulated, has resulted in the growth of a bureaucracy whose standards are double, whose rules are incomprehensible, and whose internal workings are chaotic.
It was said by the Prime Minister that all Canadians would have to tighten their belts and fight inflation together. Unfortunately the Anti-Inflation Board evidently failed to get this message, for it has been allowing far more generous pay increases in the public sector than in private industry.
A Financial Times survey of 104 wage decisions made by the board shows this divergence clearly. The survey showed 69 per cent of workers in the public sector have been allowed increases of 20 per cent or more, while raises for 79 per cent of employees in the private sector have been held to 15 per cent or less. In fact most decisions handed down from Ottawa have been in line with the pace of wage settlements before last October when the board was created.
This situation is particularly true for public sector employees who in several recent cases have won pay increases of 20 per cent or more, even through the guidelines the board is supposed to enforce allow first-year pay raises of little more than 10 per cent. The Times goes on to say that during the whole of 1975 wage settlements averaged 19 per cent for government employees and 14.2 per cent in the private sector. This is the situation the AntiInflation Board was brought in to control last October, with the wage ceiling set at a maximum 10 per cent for this year.

An analysis of 104 cases involving 57,000 workers meriting special consideration shows that in the case of first-year wage settlements the board has approved: Firstly, wage increases of 20 per cent or more for 15,000 public servants, most of them employees of Ontario school boards; and, secondly, wage rises of 15 per cent or more for 7,500 private sector workers; and pay hikes in about the same range as last year's settlements, 10 per cent to 15 per cent, for another 27,000 employees in private sector cases. A mere 1,000 private sector workers and only 500 government workers have been held to the government's intended guideline of a 10 per cent salary advance. Although the government is claiming that the board is achieving considerable results, it might pay to look more closely at these results.
Were it not for the drastic drop in food costs there would have been little or no improvement, and the minister and his colleagues would do well to resist the temptation to assume that the battle against inflation is half won. Although food prices at the farm gate are not controlled, the Anti-Inflation Board still claims some of the credit. It says controls on the profits of food processors and supermarkets helped keep prices down. That is possible, but I suggest the key element in the reduction of food costs has been a drastic drop in beef prices at the farm gate because of excess of supply.
I will come to the matter of confusion surrounding the Anti-Inflation Board rules in a moment, but first I think something should be said about the confusing bureaucracy from which these rules emanate.
In October last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) declared the board's staff would total less than 200. Today the board's staff stands at 600 and appears to be still growing. Board officials maintain that this merely reflects problems of the start-up period and that this figure will in fact drop sometime in the future, but no one knows when. In the interim they insist that the board is not now operating in excess of the 398 man-years it was allowed because some 200 employees are on loan from other departments. That comment is rather lame, however, since the salaries of those borrowed employees must be paid by the AntiInflation Board.
So far as accomplishment is concerned, the latest figures show that the board has processed 2,304 of the 6,139 cases submitted to it. The backlog of 3,845 cases is growing at the rate of an additional 150 a week. These figures are for the wage side of the business. On the prices side of things, only 179 of 1,040 compliance forms received have been processed.
What would be amusing, if it weren't so sad, is the fact that the board's present workload and backlog do not yet include the impact of the additional 41,000 companies which the government recently brought under the controls. With figures such as these in mind it would be hoped that the board would present a cohesive and efficient organization to handle the responsibilities which have been so casually imposed on it. This, unfortunately, does not seem to be the case. For example, in the April 26 Financial Times it is reported:
April 27, 1976

There has ... been considerable turnover at the most senior administrative levels and some insiders say the organization is far from crisp.
'We're constantly flying by the seat of our pants', says one official. 'Everything is improvisation, which is inevitable because we had to start from scratch with the vaguest of guidelines. But under pressure the decision-making sometimes gets so slap-dash that it's frightening.'
Another official stated, 'The organization is still pretty hectic. People come and go, bringing their own ideas and approaches. That means things still tend to change from day to day.'
As a result of this situation and the increase in the number of the employees of the AIB, the Public Service Commission now is looking to its executive interchange program to find 60 or 70 professional accountants whose employers might be willing to loan them for a year.
As an illustration of the way business feels about the regulations they have been handed, I quote this excerpt from an article in Executive Magazine entitled "Chaos Rules at the Anti-Inflation Board":
Employers already have spent enough time studying the regulations to realize that the rules at best are unclear, and, at worst, are totally incomprehensible. To take just one example, manufacturers are faced with three different rules in figuring out the maximum profit they will be allowed. The problem is in determining the appropriate rule to apply in each part of their business. The regulations provide a process of elimination, based on the extent to which the company can allocate its costs to separate items of production. If you can allocate costs to individual products, then you use one rule. If you can't do this but you can allocate costs to individual classes or lines of products, then you use another rule, and so on. The trouble is that this selection procedure is a concoction of economic theory and bears little relation to normal business practices-the test is not whether a company actually does allocate its costs in the specified ways, but whether it can do so.
And every single manufacturer in Canada meets that requirement-it can allocate its costs to every individual product, even though the method of doing so might be crude or unrealistic. To take the regulations literally, all the other rules of profit calculation would be irrelevant. The next step is to start digging through the Anti-Inflation Board's interpretation bulletins for clarification, on the assumption that the government must have had some reason for including those other two rules. This isn't the place to discuss in detail what the relevant bulletin has to say. But it has the effect of making it almost impossible for a company to use the first rule. At this stage the bemused company abandons the written rules and turns to the AntiInflation Board staff for help. The fact that even the accounting and legal experts are having such difficulties in making sense of the regulations should help to identify the most serious and possibly fatal flaw in the entire anti-inflation program. The government forgot that it was not writing a new Income Tax Act. To design its new system, it hired people in the business of either finding or closing loopholes in the tax system-in other words, tax experts from both inside and outside government. These wizards drew on their wealth of experience and concocted the predictable brew: a maze to beat all mazes, a monstrosity guaranteed to remain undeciphered for years after the anti-inflation program goes out of existence.
Of course the Anti-Inflation Board cannot hope to be the complete answer to Canada's economic ills. The government has continually refused to recognize that different monetary and fiscal policies must also be adopted, as well as an improved viewpoint on the part of government itself.
Government is the single greatest contributor to Canada's domestic inflation. Rather than control its own skyrocketing spending and growth patterns, it continues to drain money away from the investor and the saver-private and corporate-to pay for its own extravagance. I do not intend to go into this aspect of the problem in any detail, Mr. Speaker, but I think that certain brief points must be made.
Anti-Inflation Act
Canada is a capital intensive country. That means that the creation of more jobs and expanded business relies heavily on the infusion of new capital in the expansion of existing commercial facilities and the creation of new ones. If this money, through severe corporate and private income tax policies, is kept from being re-invested, then Canada's inflation and unemployment problems can in the long run be expected to become worse.
In conclusion I think it must be recognized that government, especially this government, has not even attempted to attack the root causes of inflation. An over-supply of money, badly conceived tax laws, and government growth are all matters that the government has refused to act upon. The Anti-Inflation Board, with all of its own inadequacies, cannot hope and should not be expected to solve the problem. At the same time the Anti-Inflation Board is the only possible means by which Canada can establish a more sensible framework for wage and price decision making. It must set targets for behaviour that can be used as a replacement for the discipline and mutual trust that only spring from the adversary system. In other words, the board is not in itself a cure for inflation. It is simply a way of cooling expectations and a means of buying time until some of the fundamental causes of inflation can be corrected.
The government has chosen to introduce a system of complex controls and to impose them for the relatively long period of three years. Both their complexity and duration are unnecessary, but the key problem facing the government is to make the program work. The Anti-Inflation Board will have to overcome some serious handicaps. It was introduced hurriedly and without a temporary freeze on prices and incomes. The result was that neither the government nor the board had the opportunity to develop a philosophical and economical framework for what it must do.
The board's first decisions have created confusion about the way in which historical wage relationships will be allowed to influence wage increases. In short, the board has failed to establish its own credibility by making decisions that are perceived as being fair and consistent. The challenge to the board must be to apply the guidelines in a way that maintains the spirit of equity. The use of mandatory wage and price controls is a new experience for Canada and we must resist the tendency to expect the controls to solve the inflation problem.
The final cure for inflation will ultimately lie in the way the government conducts its stabilization policies-monetary policy, energy policy and fiscal policy. It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I urge the House to consider favourably the amendments presented by the hon. member for York-Simcoe.

There has been some improvement in the cost of living index, but as has been stated before this is only evident in the price of food, and if there were no drastic drop in the food component of the cost of living index there would have been little or no improvement in the index. One of the key elements, even in food costs, has been the drastic drop of beef prices at the farm gate. This has come about only because the beef industry is now in a state of liquidation and the herds in North America are being scaled down to a level consistent with the market, which has put many beef producers out of business. Most experts in the cattle industry feel that the price of beef should be nearly 50 per cent higher to make it once more profitable. Therefore in the long run so far as beef is concerned the present drop in the price is unlikely to remain down for many months.
Public acceptance of AIB actions has by no means been unanimous. Obviously unionized labour, as has been well documented, has taken an antagonistic view and has withdrawn from the Canada Relations Council, the body on which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) put so much emphasis as a means of preventing disruptive strikes.
Professionals are also finding it difficult to comply with the regulations, and while there will be no organized confrontation with the government there is no doubt that their productivity will fall to a certain extent. Although we may decry what organized labour is doing, we have to realize that it represents a very important segment of our community, a segment which is vital to our national economy. They represent the mining and transportation industries, to name but a few, and they are necessary to produce the goods that Canada needs to export to preserve its standard of living. There seems to be no doubt that AIB regulations will dampen the productivity of many Canadians, particularly in the vital goods segments of our economy.
It has been increasingly recognized that there is not much point in curtailing wages and prices if it is going to

result in decreased productivity in our industrial and export segment. People in the Economic Council of Canada who have studied the Canadian labour market have found significant indications of where the increases in wages have concentrated in our economy. Between 1961 and 1974 substantial modernization and productivity gains occurred in agriculture, forestry, and mining. Real plant and equipment per person employed increased by over 80 per cent in all three industries, compared with 30 per cent in manufacturing and less than 5 per cent in the wholesale and retail trades. This process involved the substitution of machines for manpower. As a result, by 1974 average hourly earnings in forestry and mining were 180 per cent and 150 per cent higher respectively than in 1961.
The construction industry recorded equally substantial wage gains. By contrast, money wage gains in the services sector by 1974 amounted to less that 120 per cent of the 1961 level. This indicates that the supply of blue-collar workers and unskilled labour to the logging camps, mines and construction sites from rural towns and farms or from abroad has shrunk measurably. In 1974, for example, weekly earnings among service workers averaged roughly 50 per cent of the earnings in construction, compared with 67 per cent in 1961. This is an important thing to consider when dealing with the Anti-Inflation Board's decisions which seem to be concentrated on rolling back wage increases in the productive goods section of our economy.
Since 1974 we have seen the loss of exports of highly manufactured goods chiefly because of the Canada-U.S. auto pact deficit and the end of the defence production sharing agreement. Export flows are now dominated by food and industrial materials. Mr. George Post, vice-chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, has said that much of the growth of exports has involved raw materials, or products in which raw materials were a significant part of the total value.
Canada also seems to be rushing headlong into the establishment of the so called post industrial society, with a majority of its work force employed in the services sector and a diminishing minority of its workers in the goods producing sector. This aspect of the change in our economy seems to be evident in the problems the AIB is having. It has been especially counterproductive in its decisions concerning wage settlements affecting the goods producing segment of our economy, such as in the now famous Irving case where the wages of workers in the pulp and paper industry were rolled back considerably. It seems to be an over-reaction by the board and, whatever its outcome, it can only damage an already hard pressed industry.
Also there has been a rollback in the wage increase by Denison and Rio Algom. The increase exceeded the guidelines but it was in line with earlier settlements reached by International Nickel and by Falconbridge. With the rollback order some workers have already began to switch to INCO and Falconbridge where they can earn $2,000 more if the rollback remains effective. This is what happened to the Wartime Prices and Incomes Board, that is, workers moved laterally in order to increase their income. Even if the AIB is supposed to observe historical wage relationships, apparently it does not recognize the importance to Denison and Rio Algom of paying competitive wages. In fact it seems obvious that AIB will have to have a much

greater knowledge about a whole lot of things of which it is seemingly unaware.
A further increase in AIB's personnel does not seem to be the answer. It is too much to expect that officials, give*n the complexities of today's business activity, can rule on the many problems with any degree of consistency or accuracy. In effect the AIB, through its government appointed administrators, is substituting for the judgments made in market place. Certainly market place judgments may not always be perfect, but they are still better than judgments made away from the market place by civil servants and by people unaware of all the circumstances of the case.
Consider the case of the Thompson mines at present. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) asked where they would go. I can tell him that they are already going to Fort McMurray. Some workers have gone to Sudbury, and many are leaving the mines to return to farming. The action of the AIB in instituting the rollback of the settlement can only cause great consternation. Even Premier Schreyer, who has not seen the light as his federal leader would want him to do, and who is an ardent supporter of controls by government, has suggested that the AIB erred. Telegrams to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the possibility of a massive group of workers descending on Ottawa to present their case indicate the workers' dismay at this ruling by AIB.
The Thompson complex contributes around 5 per cent of the total economic activity in the province of Manitoba. If the workings of this complex are seriously compromised, it can only be described as disastrous for the economy of Manitoba and the economy of Canada in the long run. The AIB again failed to take into account the historical relationship of INCO of Manitoba with Sudbury, and already INCO of Manitoba is losing some of its workers to INCO in Sudbury.
One of the most disturbing features of the AIB actions has been its tendencies to exert its powers to control wages in that segment of our economy which produces the goods to fuel the progress of our economy, particularly exports.
In an article in the Financial Times of Canada of April 26 statistics were produced to show that the AIB has been far more generous in increases for the public sector than in the private sector. They made a survey of 104 wage decisions reached by the board. It indicates that 69 per cent of public sector workers had been allowed increases of 20 per cent or more, while raises for 79 per cent of employees in the private sector have been held to 15 per cent or more.
Furthermore, the survey raises the question of whether the board is able to influence wage settlements as the awards handed down from Ottawa have been in line with the pace of wage settlements before last October when the board was created. A notable example which I mentioned previously was pointed out. The wage contract of Denmi-son Mines was cut from 16.8 per cent to 10.9 per cent, although the historical relationship with other workers was acknowledged and the firms were known to hold and contract skilled employees. On the same day the board announced an approval of a 16 per cent salary raise for employees of the Dryden board of education. Indeed it is
Anti-Inflation Act
becoming increasingly doubtful whether the board is in any way reducing inflation. In fact, it may be making it more likely.
When the government has aimed for an inflationary target of 8 per cent, the board has allowed raises in excess of 10 per cent, and in over half the cases raises of over 15 per cent. The board seems to be rolling back wages in the goods producing sector, upon which we rely, in favour of the service sector. It is felt generally at the present time that our goods producing sector is not functioning as well as it should.
I should like to speak for a moment about the problems of professionals. No matter what way the attempt is made to control professionals, it seems to me that it will be at best a very indiscriminate operation. Most professionals will obey the AIB guidelines, but they will obey them by reducing the amount of productivity they could attain. It is better to take a month off than run the risk of having not only the results of all the extra effort confiscated, but to find that there is a severe penalty for that extra productivity. Obviously in many instances professionals will have increased their incomes by more than $2,400, and this would include those who have stayed rigidly within the guidelines or who work in schedules set by the provincial governments.
Some of the problems professionals will run into are becoming obvious. Let us consider the example of a professional in my province of Manitoba. The AIB ruled that professionals who practise under the various government schemes and who, for example, are not opted out physicians, will come under the safe haven rule, and they will have minimum compliance regulations with perhaps a nominal reporting record. However, for those physicians who may have opted out of the provincial scheme although there may not be any greater charge than the provincial paying agency is making, the AIB has indicated that it intends to throw the book at them and pursue them energetically in order to make sure that they do not overstep the income guidelines. In doing this the board is following the advice of the government of Manitoba which does not like opted out physicians and other like professionals. I think that is an indication that those who are in practice outside, or those who are on their own, will fare much worse than those who have remained within the government fold.
Much depends on the forms which will be issued to professionals. Almost certainly they will be so complicated that the AIB officials will be able to convict or find a professional guilty under almost any circumstance. By and large, professionals will be at a considerable disadvantage because they will not be able to afford the large battery of accountants and legal advisors which large concerns are able to have at their command. To a large extent the individual professional will be controlled by the corresponding officials in the AIB who will, in many cases, have to make a fairly arbitrary decision because it seems obvious that it would be almost impossible to break down the income and arrive at a fair assessment. I would not blame the offical for this, but this is just the nature of the problem.
The limit of $2,400 may seem to be fair and equitable because professionals on the whole do make good incomes,

but on closer examination it will probably be counter productive. In the province of Manitoba, which has the highest income tax in Canada, an individual making over $28,000 per year retains only 37 per cent of his extra income, so that out of a $2,400 increase he will, in effect, retain a little over $900. If he had an income gross before tax of $30,000 with a net take home pay of perhaps $16,000, with only a $900 per year increase he has lost considerably in his actual income. There certainly would be no point in his continuing to increase his productivity, and he would have to organize himself so that his income would fall below the $2,400 increase, or at least not above it. The balance of his efforts would be directed into other fields such as more holidays, more hobby work, more time spent for his own personal enjoyment. This might be a good thing for the individual concerned, but I doubt if it is very valuable for the economy of the country.
I believe this legislation will be a disaster when the final assessment is made. It certainly seems to discourage productivity, and we have a problem of Canadians investing outside Canada. There has been a trend in the last few years toward greater investment outside Canada by Canadians, particularly in the United States. I support very strongly the idea that this legislation should be reviewed in 18 months, with the possibility that it be terminated, Certainly 18 months is long enough for this legislation to be in effect before it is reassessed.

I cannot imagine any man in the position of the Minister of Finance, or anyone on the Treasury benches, setting out upon a program without taking stock. I realize the minister had problems back last October when he was in a kafuffle and did not know where he was going or what form the program would take. They hustled it through the House and through committee. Had they at least taken stock at committee stage last fall and listened to some of the suggestions of members of the official opposition we would not be back in the House tonight debating Bill C-89.
I ask the minister, instead of hustling this bill through tonight, instead of hustling the amendment through, would he not now stop and take stock? I can assure him that the affairs of this nation are of interest to the opposition parties as well as to the government. We will help. We will give the kind of concrete and sensible suggestions and amendments that will make the program work.
When we pause to take stock of where we are today we find there has been no progress, no improvement in economic conditions in Canada. I shall not speak on the effects on labour as I think the position of labour and the rough justice meted out to it have been well expounded already.
So far there have been only three rulings by the AntiInflation Board in regard to prices. How can we talk about the success, or the appearance of success of the program when in fact there have only been three rulings? The Leader of the New Democratic party pointed them out- indeed I believe he only pointed out two, Esso and beer. Being a man of abstinence and not consuming alcoholic beverages, that latter one does not concern me. We would have to say, however, that there has not been any progress so far as restraining prices is concerned.

In the election back in the spring of 1974 the prices and incomes policy that this party suggested was to be for only 18 months and was to begin with a 90 day freeze, a period that would allow the government to put into place a program to fight inflation. I think it is agreed by most economists and most members of this House that the government's price and wage control program, or anti-inflation program, does not in itself have any effect on the causes of inflation. But the causes themselves must be attacked, Mr. Speaker. In taking stock surely the minister must have in mind programs that would get to the root causes of inflation.
The whole area of money supply has been discussed in this House previously. As a concrete suggestion I urge the minister to take some time to consider the position of Milton Friedman who suggests that inflation is always a special and monetary phenomenon. He stresses the impact of an abnormally high growth in the money supply and translates that into the effect on falling trade and the surplus of Canadian funds outside Canada, particularly in a time when there is an unfavourable balance of trade. We are facing a trade deficit of around $5 billion this year. Milton Friedman has a great deal more to say about this matter and I wish the minister would take heed of it.
I believe we need a responsible and realistic policy on money supply. I am not advocating zero growth in money supply, Mr. Speaker. I realize that a growth of 7 per cent or 8 per cent is necessary, and I realize what follows a tight money supply but surely the minister understands what follows if you have an accelerated or abnormally high rate growth of money supply such as we are having now, of 16 per cent or 18 per cent.
If we are to get at the roots of inflation I should think the minister would want to take stock of his fiscal policy. I know that speeches are often made in this Chamber that are frankly political in nature. On this side of the House at least we do not participate in that kind of political partisanship, but nevertheless it sometimes appears in the House. Notwithstanding that, it seems to me that a fiscal policy ought to be at least consistent with the kind of restraint that the government expects from the Canadian people.
I think it is wrong that the government expects the wage earner to restrain his income to increases of 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 12 per cent, depending on whether the historical relationship clause applies, while on the other hand it allows government expenditures to rise to 16 per cent, without the effect of supplementary estimates.
I have some sympathy with those economists who say that a tight fiscal policy will have some negative effects on unemployment. But, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to talk about the negative effect of a real restraint policy such as federal spending on unemployment, then we also have to take into consideration the recent report of the Economic Council of Canada tabled in this House. That report suggested that the $4 billion to be spent on unemployment insurance this year ought to be tied to productivity. The report made some concrete suggestions, and I know that many who served on the Economic Council of Canada would have liked to have made the recommendations far stronger and far more decisive than the watered down recommendations that finally appeared in the report.
Anti-Inflation Act
I would ask the minister to take stock of the non-productivity of the unemployment insurance program and tie it back to productivity. The Economic Council of Canada had a great deal to say about the effect of productivity on international trade and our trade balance and competitive position in respect of world trade. I ask the Minister of Finance to take stock, not of this piecemeal, fly as you go, on the job training, but of the total program that reflects the studies, positions and suggestions, not only of opposition members but of people across the nation. I might make one suggestion to the minister. Perhaps he ought to fire all the economists on his staff, save one. At least then he would only be confused once.
When we consider the effects of the anti-inflation program, and particularly the amendment before us in relation to Bill C-89 which deals with the time element for the law of the land to be effective, it is important to point out that we in the opposition are not talking about the termination of the program. We ought not to be fooled or misled into believing that all we want is a commitment from the government in respect to the anti-inflation program. That would be deceiving.
It is not the program that we necessarily want ended because the program itself is arbitrary and can be changed by order in council. The existing law of the land allows the cabinet to write their own policy, and it can change day by day. The provisions of Bill C-73, which is now the law of the land, in no way specifies, outlines, details or establishes, except in the widest parameters, the specifics of the program. Therefore we are not asking for assurance in so far as the existing program is concerned because it can be changed. What we are asking is that the law of the land terminate in a year.
We on this side are not unreasonable. If in a year's time the government's program is working and it is getting in place the programs it ought to be getting in place, it will not only be helped by the Canadian people but by members on this side. We will give it the full measure of credit. If at that time the weight of argument warrants an extension of the program, we will be prepared to give that kind of extension. However, in the true parliamentary tradition, we stand opposed to the open-endedness of this kind of arbitrary legislation.
If the legislation were specific, that would be one matter, but it is not. It is arbitrary in so far as I pointed out that it is really a prerogative of the cabinet. It is that kind of arbitrary power which is not consistent with the parliamentary tradition. We have precedents for this kind of openended approach to legislation in our Defence Production Act. The former leader of my party made reference to that last fall when we were first discussing the anti-inflation program.
In conclusion, when this House recesses for the day, I ask the minister to find some corner of an office and, in the solitude of that moment, reflect upon the program and take the kind of stock I have been asking him to take. I ask him to give consideration to accepting some suggestions. The members on this side are sincerely interested in getting to the roots of inflation. Get a policy in place to fight inflation. We are prepared to accept the rough justice for a

Our party has taken the position that, notwithstanding the blemishes in the plan, we ought to give the government a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate it will work over a reasonable period of time. Thus, while we support the plan we consider ourselves free, in the meantime, to draw attention to what we consider to be its deficiencies.
As I pointed out on second reading, if we ever get into a situation of the kind to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) alluded in his remarks at the end of last year, if we get into a system of permanent controls or an altogether different economic system in Canada, it would be very easy indeed for the government to abdicate its responsibility in the area of fiscal and monetary measures and rely exclusively on a system of controls which, I suggest, would not get at the root causes of inflation and would bring about more problems than it solves.
It seems to me, if I may say so without imputing motives, that the government is attempting to gain the benefit of the traditional advantage inherent in Canada's relationship with the United States-that of sharing any upturn in the U.S. economy. After all, between 60 and 70 per cent of our trade is carried on with the United States, and it is my impression that in bringing forward this program the government had in mind the hope that the economy will follow the trend in the United States, that the rate of inflation here will decline. Things are promising for our neighbours south of the border, and indeed I believe the prospects are not all that bad for us-we may experience an upturn here; all hon. members, I am sure, hope that the inflation rate will go down and that our economy will prosper. In any case we can do a great deal to help by limiting the period of application of wage and price controls. I ask the minister to give serious consideration to placing a limit on this program.
When I read the statistics with respect to the terrific backlog of cases now facing the Anti-Inflation Board I can only conclude that the proposal put forward by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe is really a favour to the government, because if this plan continues for any considerable period of time it will be necessary to extend the scope of the scheme, expand the administration, and increase the size of the bureaucracy required to operate the system.
When the program began it was said the total number of staff likely to be needed by the Board would not exceed 200 persons. On the basis of the figures now available with respect to the backlog it appears it will be necessary to increase that figure very substantially-not tenfold, not even twentyfold, but a hundredfold in due course if the plan is allowed to carry on for an unreasonable length of time as suggested in Bill C-73. That is why the proposal put forward by my hon. friend from York-Simcoe is one which should be embraced by the government; it would permit it to break away from this program and get rid of it within a reasonable period.
I want to direct these remarks to the minister, since he is here, and to indicate my sympathy with the Leader of the
April 27, 1976

New Democratic Party in the unfortunate position in which he finds himself, one which makes him uneasy and nervous since he has to justify his own position as leader of a national party on one hand while trying to support the position of his colleagues in the provincial parties on the other. I must say, though, that I agree with him to this extent: the program is ill-conceived and should probably not be supported for the period originally intended. We should face the issue and say that now is the time to bring the program to an end.
As I say, the problem we face now is the program's lack of credibility. The indication I have received as a result of questionnaires put out among my constituents is that while they support an anti-inflation program they have great difficulty in accepting the veracity and good faith of the government with respect to its actions; they find it difficult to understand the reason for the continuous and continued growth in government expenditures and the fact that government expenditures do not seem to be subject to the same rules as are expenditures in the private sector; they find it difficult to reconcile the government's calls for restraint with the increase in its own spending. So I say, in all sincerity, that if the Minister of Finance really wishes to do a service to his portfolio and to his country he will use his influence with the Prime Minister and his other colleagues, as well as with his caucus, to secure support for my hon. friend's motion. I personally feel it is worthy of support.

I recall very vividly a question it directed to us during the last election campaign: what are you going to do when the control period ends? Now, of course, it has that problem itself.
One of the points that we disliked very much in Bill C-73, the original anti-inflation legislation, was the open-ended provision whereby the legislation could be extended indefinitely by order in council. To us, Mr. Speaker, this sounded like permanent controls, and to people across the country who were broadly concerned about controls it also sounded like permanent controls. Recent comments by columnists and various commentators in this country on the progress of the anti-inflation program have confirmed that, in their view as well, this program is one of permanent controls. I believe the labour movement generally perceives it to be a program of permanent controls, which is why it is so opposed to it.
Anti-Inflation Act
I believe only seven out of the ten provinces of Canada are committed to the anti-inflation program, and I think that without exception those provinces that are have placed a limit on their commitment. I understand that this is 18 months, though in one case I believe it is 24 months. Gefterally speaking I think we can say that the provinces want the program to end after 18 months.
In Bill C-89, which motion No. 1 is endeavouring to amend, there is provision to end the program prior to December 31, 1978, and I have been wondering why that provision is in the bill. Obviously it is in the bill to give the government the option of ending the program providing it finds a way to slip out of it easily and knows what to do when the program has ended.
The matter that really concerns me is this: we started out with three main points. There was an export levy, a limit on profits-and by a mathematical calculation that was supposed to control prices-and, of course, we had a limit on wage increases. Why the export levy was imposed at the very beginning is something I shall never understand, but however it has been removed. We now see a great deal of pressure building in the business community to modify the profit control provision or remove it. As a matter of fact the minister stated, I understand, that he is prepared to look at this question in October of this year. If that section of the act is extensively modified, then the only thing left is wage controls, and I do not think that is acceptable. It may be acceptable to some people, but I do not think that generally across the country it will be acceptable and that the legislation can continue if it controls only wages. There is the dilemma that we are facing.
I understand that the leader of the NDP, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), has moved an amendment that would end the legislation on May 1 1976.

I think it is generally agreed today by those who have carefully studied the program, even by people in the AntiInflation Board itself, that had there been a 90 day freeze at the very beginning-and I think the reason there was not a 90 day freeze is that it would have been an absolute copy of the main recommendations that we made and it was just too hard for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to swallow that-then the program may have had a better chance of succeeding than it has right now. However, the

Anti-Inflation Act
Leader of the New Democratic Party, in order to try to remain a little bit credible to his people, says we are not being consistent in asking for a May 1, 1977, end to the program. It is he who is not being consistent, as he rarely is in many of the things upon which he comments.
The concern of people across the country to whom I have talked-and I have travelled a fair bit talking to quite a few people in labour and business-is that we are in a real decline. We are not pulling out of our recession. We see countries around us, like the United States, making really significant gains in their economy. We see more people being employed; we see a prime rate of 5'A per cent in the U.S., and we see a great deal of industrial activity taking place. One of the things I always watch for very closely is orders being placed for machine tools, and I think they are at their highest level now for several years. That is an indication of industrial activity down the road. Some of us who recently visited Japan saw a definite movement in their economy as well. Though they are planning for a slow growth period to about 1985, there is a definite movement and they are making progress.
In each of these countries, as well as others that have had control programs, it was found that the best way to control inflation is by means of good, strong fiscal and monetary policies. I know that those words have rolled out of the mouth of every politician in the country for several months now, but if you take politics out of it and look at inflation without politics this seems to be the solution that most countries have favoured.
I do not believe we are making much progress in this regard in Canada. We find our interest rates are high. This makes it difficult for businessmen to borrow money to expand their plant. We find a limit placed on profits and we find little effect on prices. This is why we feel the program should end on May 1, 1977, after an 18 month period. It has not gone the way we would have liked but it has been an interesting experiment. I think it has had some restraining influence; most of the provinces have cut back on their budgets.
Speaking in Toronto the other day the minister mentioned that if the provinces and municipalities would cut back on their budgets the anti-inflation program would have a much greater effect. A number of them have done this, and are endeavouring to continue next year and down the road. Perhaps the lesson of inflation has been learned by a great number of people. Having had this experience for 18 months, then I think we should end this on May 1, 1977. That is why I support the motion. subtopic: TRANSPORT-ATLANTIC REGION-MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS ON HIGHWAY PROGRAM- TRANS-NEWFOUNDLAND CORRIDOR STUDY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
TRANSPORT-ATLANTIC REGION-MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS ON HIGHWAY PROGRAM- TRANS-NEWFOUNDLAND CORRIDOR STUDY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) is here. I had hoped he would
Adjournment Debate
have attended the committee but I knew he had to be in the House. I hope his very capable district director will be able to influence him regarding the very excellent presentation I made on behalf of the lobster fishermen of Newfoundland.
Let me get to the point of the debate tonight which has to do with transportation. On March 29 I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) because of my concern about the deterioration of the highway system in the province of Newfoundland and in the Atlantic region generally. I had in mind particularly the presentation by the ministers of highways and transport ministers of the Atlantic region regarding a highways improvement or strengthening program, similar to those presented in briefs by other provinces of Canada. The minister in reply indicated that his discussions with the provincial ministers related more to the issue of support for the movement of freight within the Atlantic region, and possibly to new programs using freight assistance more adequately for the development and improvement of the Atlantic region.
The minister also in his reply confirmed that a brief had been presented on highway strengthening and indicated that he would undertake a further examination of the brief before responding. Just today I had occasion to present the problem to the Canadian Transport Commission at the hearings of the transport committee, and in my representation I referred to the Trans-Newfoundland Transportation Corridor Study which made certain recommendations in compliance with the very objectives I preach tonight.
In addressing myself to the problem, and to the parliamentary secretary who represents the minister, I say there is a deliberate thrust by the CNR to downgrade rail freight and express service in Newfoundland. I suggest it is just as deliberate as was the thrust to downgrade the rail passenger service in that province back in 1969. Evidence exists that the CNR is deliberately moving to road transport in spite of denials to the contrary. There is evidence that traffic loadings are decreasing to justify the lay-off of personnel. Statistics prove that loadings in Newfoundland are increasing and yet the CNR is moving to road transport. At the same time the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland is being overtaxed by increases in rubber traffic. There have been increases in the last five years of almost 1,000 per cent, much of which is due to the fact that the CNR is contributing to that effort.
At the moment the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland is deteriorating to the point of no return, in fact to the point where soon it will be dangerous for persons to drive their cars on the highway because of the increase in road traffic. This is as a result of the increase in container traffic and the traffic which is being released from the rail traffic which we have in abundance. I say it is a condemnation of the government and the Ministry of Transport that the situation has been allowed to develop as it has today. Nothing is being done about it.
It further disturbs me to read news releases to the effect that many millions, indeed billions of dollars are being provided in other provinces to strengthen highways, to provide road link-ups, and to provide access roads for the development of the rural and industrial economy.

For some reason or other those who profess to know are ignorant of what is required by all regions of the nation to provide a basis for our economy. It becomes increasingly obvious that the province of Newfoundland will wait until all other provinces are looked after in respect of Canada's transportation needs.
The Atlantic region transportation ministers have submitted a brief to the Minister of Transport requesting support for the needs of Atlantic Canada. I would appreciate it if the parliamentary secretary would give me some hope concerning his minister's intentions to show that the Atlantic region, and particularly the province of Newfoundland, are still part of Canada. I hope he will indicate that Newfoundland will receive its just due in the contribution that our central government makes not only in respect of a strengthening program for its highways but more important in respect of the need for a recommendation concerning a transport system not only from Vancouver to Halifax but indeed to the province of Newfoundland.
