subtopic: TRANSPORT-ATLANTIC REGION-MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL MINISTERS ON HIGHWAY PROGRAM- TRANS-NEWFOUNDLAND CORRIDOR STUDY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire very much indeed to provide my hon. friend with some of the hope to which he alluded in the final moments of his remarks this evening. Further to the comments he has made both tonight and in this House on March 29, I should perhaps remind the House that it was on March 10, 1976, that the highway ministers of the four Atlantic provinces first presented a joint report to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) which is entitled "Atlantic Provinces Primary Highways-Ten Year Program". This report is a statement of needs as seen by the provinces and was prepared subsequent to previous meetings between the provincial ministers and the Minister of Transport. The report is presently under study by departmental personnel in the Ministry of Transport.
With regard to recent highway expenditures in the Atlantic region, these have been made mainly through special and subsidiary agreements between the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the respective provinces. In this connection it is interesting to note that in 1974-75 federal highway expenditures amounted to $18.2 million in Newfoundland, $1.3 million in Prince Edward Island, $1.4 million in Nova Scotia, and $18.1 million in New Brunswick. It is likely that 1975-76 expenditures will be in the same order of magnitude.
Concerning the standardization of truck weights we have now reached the point where these are all now at a minimum of 20,000 pounds for a single axle load with the exception of Newfoundland where the figure is 18,000, and at a minimum gross vehicle weight of 110,000 pounds, with the exception of Nova Scotia where it is 80,000 pounds. Completion of standardization of loads limits can be expected to result in increased economies for truck transportation which is one of the objectives of the federal Ministry of Transport and, I am sure, of the provincial ministers involved.
With regard to rail freight and express service in Newfoundland, may I assure the hon. member that every effort is being made to provide adequate rail service to shippers and receivers in this area. The CNR has undertaken a number of initiatives recommended in the trans-Newfoundland corridor transportation study completed in 1974

to improve the transportation system. These actions include the construction of a new express freight shed at Cornerbrook, increased capacity of the rail car wheel-set transfer operation at Port aux Basques, and the establishment of a freight planning group in St. John's to improve the scheduling of traffic.
In general, and in conclusion, I want to assure my hon. friend that the Government of Canada has substantially supported Atlantic region transportation and will continue to do so in the future.

subtopic: FINANCE-SUGGESTED CHANGES IN EQUALIZATION FORMULA AS RESULT OF INCREASED ENERGY COSTS- REQUEST FOR REPORT
FINANCE-SUGGESTED CHANGES IN EQUALIZATION FORMULA AS RESULT OF INCREASED ENERGY COSTS- REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps very appropriate that my question, following the one of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), should deal with energy because I think the two problems that are plaguing the Atlantic economy right now are the great and continuing difficulties we have had with transportation and transportation costs and with energy and the great impact which rising energy costs have had on the Atlantic region in the last three years.
Hon. members will recall that on April 5 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) whether, in view of the meeting of the first ministers that was taking place that week, there would be some consultations with ministers from the Atlantic provinces with respect to the suggestion of the minister of finance in Ontario, Mr. McKeough, who had suggested that there might be a consideration of some alteration in the equalization formula, particularly with respect to the skyrocketing electrical costs in the two provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. To a lesser degree, of course, this affects Newfoundland and New Brunswick, and I think it has some impact as well on one or two of the provinces in western Canada.
The Minister of Finance at that time was not able to give me that assurance. He said he would be discussing the matter generally with his colleagues but that this might be a question which could be resolved prior to the meeting of first ministers on energy at the beginning of next month. Therefore it is doubly appropriate that I raise this question tonight because in a little more than a week's time that meeting of first ministers will take place.
However, it is extremely disturbing to be raising the question following the announcement of the energy policy by the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) this afternoon. To my mind the statement by the minister this afternoon showed an almost complete lack of awareness or sensitivity to the energy problems of Atlantic Canada. When the minister indicated this afternoon that eventually there would be a move on his part to raise the price of domestic oil to international levels, and that one of the purposes of increasing domestic energy prices would be to reinforce efficiency and conservation, it seemed to me that the minister was trying to make a virtue out of the hardship that will obviously be created for many of the people already living on low incomes, some of the lowest incomes in the country, and in those regions in the country that can least afford to protect themselves.
April 27, 1976

Quite frankly, I was shocked at the insensitivity of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in suggesting that. It is similar, of course, to the further part of the answer which the Minister of Finance gave me on April 5 when I asked about some assistance with respect to the conversion from expensive electrical generation to lower cost forms of electrical production. The answer of the Minister of Finance referred quite specifically to nuclear power and the CANDU reactor, particularly the one which is contemplated for New Brunswick, yet the Pointe Lepreau reactor, when it comes on stream, will produce something like 600 megawatts compared with the estimated potential of the Fundy tidal power operation, which could produce something like 4,000 megawatts.
When we examine the statement of the minister this afternoon there is no mention of the possibility of proceeding as quickly as possible with Fundy tidal power development. There was certainly no mention of it by the Minister of Finance the other day, even though he must be well acquainted with its potential, having served in the portfolio of Energy, Mines and Resources.
All in all we are faced with a situation in which there seems to be no awareness yet by the government that there are consumers and producers living in my province of Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia who are paying as much as 200 per cent to 300 per cent more for their electricity than those who live in parts of southern Ontario, or even in some parts of the province of Quebec. This further emphasis on disparity and economic and social hardship for the people of the Atlantic provinces is unacceptable, and quite frankly I find it illogical. The government, having moved some time ago to standardize a base price for the cost of petroleum products, whether it be in eastern or western Canada, is now making the assumption that what it can do in one area with respect to petroleum it cannot do in another, and that is in the area of electical generation and electrical costs.
If there is to be a consistent approach in this respect, and if the government believes that one price for petroleum products should be established, even if that price is an increased one, as was suggested by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources this afternoon-but it would be a price which would be equal and fair for consumers from coast to coast-surely the logic of that, which I think has been generally accepted on all sides of this House and by all Canadians, is equally true with something as basic as electricity costs. I think it is an absolute farce for a government to expend something like $500 million in an attempt to reduce the disparities which exist between the poor and the rich regions of this country and then say that it is in no position whatsoever to act with respect to the enormous burdens which are being placed on the backs of consumers in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and the other poorer provinces. I hope the parliamentary secretary can give us a definite assurance tonight that this kind of insensitivity and illogical approach which is presently being taken will in fact be altered at the first ministers' meeting.

Quebec is in a similar situation.
The federal government is aware of the problem in the Maritime provinces and it has taken certain steps to rectify it. The hon. member may not be aware of all the efforts made by the federal government to help the Maritime provinces has concerns energy supplies.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF GUN CONTROL MEASURE TO SUPREME COURT TO DETERMINE WHETHER JURISDICTION FEDERAL OR PROVINCIAL
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF GUN CONTROL MEASURE TO SUPREME COURT TO DETERMINE WHETHER JURISDICTION FEDERAL OR PROVINCIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I seem a little out of breath it is because I just ran over from the committee that is considering Bill C-83.
I want to deal tonight with questions I asked on April 6, 1976, as reported at page 12501 of Hansard when I put this question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Justice. It is with regard to the Di Iorio and Gerard Fontaine case in which the Supreme Court of Canada held that the provincial government should have the right to conduct a criminal inquiry within the terms "administration of justice of the province".
This bill is now before the committee and if anybody had heard the proceedings at committee tonight they would wonder how the bill ever got out of this House-except by closure. From page 47 to page 53 the bill deals in brief with the fact that the federal government is giving power to the provinces to investigate crime and hold criminal inquiries. The fact is, however, that the Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that the province of Quebec, and any other province, under our constitution has that power. That means that when this bill left this House through closure, eight of its pages were redundant because the provincial governments already had the power it proposed to give to them.
I should like to read briefly from the judgment of Mr. Justice Pigeon of the Supreme Court of Canada. At page 13 he said:
If it must be said that such an inquiry prior to any charge being laid under the Criminal Code comes within the description of "administration of justice in the province", not of "procedure in a criminal matter", I cannot appreciate how one may take a different view where the object of the inquiry ...
In other words, the province of Quebec had that power. I should now like to read from page 14 of the judgment where he says that under the British North America Act the administration of justice falls under provincial jurisdiction but questions of criminal law fall under the ambit of federal jurisdiction. The judge said:
... "administration of justice" in all matters civil and criminal, which has consistently been held to include the detection of criminal activities.
He held that this falls within the admit of the provinces.
I should like to read from the judgment of Mr. Justice Dickson of the same court, who said:
First, I cannot subscribe to the view that administration of criminal justice is for parliament alone to prescribe.
It is also for the provinces. I would also like to quote from page 12 where the same judge said:
It seems late in the day to strip the provinces of jurisdiction in respect of criminal justice which they have exercised without challenge for well over 100 years.
Part of that bill now deals with provincial inquiries. It has gone to a committee for study. The Supreme Court of Canada in its judgment constitutionally says that lower is well within the ambit of the province of Quebec. If it had not been for its inquiry we would never have found out that carcasses were being sawed up, ground, and turned into hamburgers at the World's Fair to be sold to the public of Canada. They had the right to make that inquiry.
It is beyond my comprehension as a parliamentarian of this House for some considerable length of time that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Liberal government would challenge the province of Quebec on the right to conduct that kind of inquiry. I can only say they wanted to cover up something they knew Quebec was bringing forth.
The main point I want to make is that two thirds of the bill dealing with control of guns is a matter of administration of justice falling within the jurisdiction of the provinces. The fact is that much of that law that says it can be done by order in council, such as the cost of licences, the administration, all of which is defined in the bill, falls within the ambit of the provinces.
I was at the committee. I wish Your Honour were on that committee because it is a big circus. The greatest defence we had was to move that the motion be not read a second time. My guess is that tomorrow morning the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will fire the Liberal members of that committee because their questions are right on. They pointed out that gun control is not only within provincial jurisdiction, but is unworkable. There are so many anomalies it will not do anything to solve crime. That is the reason why I asked that question.
Bill C-83 was produced for one reason. It is a legal poultice to try to get the Canadian people to believe that the government is doing something to solve crime and to cover up the fact that it brought in a bill only two and a half years ago regarding penalties for murder which it will not carry out. I end with this sentence. This bill is to cover up for the fact that the government will not carry out the law that it brought in with reference to murder.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-SUGGESTED REFERENCE OF GUN CONTROL MEASURE TO SUPREME COURT TO DETERMINE WHETHER JURISDICTION FEDERAL OR PROVINCIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I am responding to my hon. friend on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and his parliamentary secretary. I am pleased to have this opportunity to do so.
As I begin, I remind the Chair and the House that I will be dealing with the substantive matters of both law and procedure which the hon. member raised in his original question in the House before the Easter adjournment. I will not direct my remarks to the rather extraneous and gratuitous references which the hon. member has made, particularly in the closing part of the speech which he just delivered.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) on April 6, 1976, asked the Minister of Justice if the government intended to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada the provisions in Bill C-83 relating to the ownership and handling of firearms for determination of their constitutional validity. The hon. member formulated his question after having referred to the recent Supreme Court decision in the cases of Di Iorio and Gerard Fontaine.

April 27, 1976

There is, of course, no relation between the Supreme Court decision in the Di Iorio and Fontaine cases and the parts of Bill C-83 relating to firearms. The Criminal Code always has had provisions dealing with guns. There has never been any suggestion that these provisions would not properly fall within the meaning of the words "criminal law" as they appear in section 91, sub-paragraph 27 of the B.N.A. Act. The proposed measures relating to guns in Bill C-83 extend and modify the existing provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with guns. It must be submitted that parliament is competent to enact such legislation as being legislation in relation to Criminal Law.
It has been held by the Privy Council and the Supreme Court of Canada that the words "criminal law" in the

constitution mean the criminal law in its widest sense. It has also been held that the power to legislate in relation to criminal law is not restricted to defining offences and providing penalties, but it also includes the power to legislate for the prevention of crime. The precise point involved here was very aptly dealt with by the Imperial Privy Council in the case of Proprietary Articles Trade Association versus the Attorney General of Canada, particularly in the judgment of Lord Atkin. His Lordship's statement is a lengthy one and I shall not take up the time of the House by quoting it in full. However, the hon. member for Calgary North is a man learned in the law and I am sure he is fully conversant with Lord Atkin's speech and will find it constructive in this connection.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.28 p.m.
